LADIES' LETTER.
Ilar DEAR NELLIE,

Very pretty hats for boating are in a modified Sailor shape, usually of burnt straw, and trimmed with a Paisley silk scarf, drawn round the crown into a bow in front. Any class of colouring may be had in these scarves, from the orange and scar- let beloved of the brunette, to the amber and tur- quoise which suit the blonde. For brightening up a shirt-blouse linen stocks are very useful. A girl can make them herself quite easily. A yard and a half, in any colour she likes, is cut into strips two inches wide, and hemmed each side. This goes twice round the neck, and ties in a sailor-knot in front. The middle part can be stiffened like a man's collar, if necessary. •

_ I have often heard remarked upon the frequeticy with which the matron wears cape manetelettes, quite short and with stole ends or Bemi-tr4ns- parent mantles, with cape backs ends, a sllor t point, quite over the arms, and with stole ecds forming a front. Bodices for the matron are finished with a point in front, and arranged in some doat fashion to open over a fussy lace vest, or a bolero top is arranged over a pointed and folded belt, 4ith cascades of lace or chiffon in front. For siich bodices the fronts are veiled, and a belt going com- pletely round the waist is avoided. Tea jackets for full figures are short behind and long and narlow in front, and foulard gowns for middle-aged wort gii have usually some species of bolero, or a flat bad:, with pleated tail, and a bolero front. Blouses for the matron have also some coat. or bolero arrange- ment in front, and the belt is narrow, and brought low pointed in front. The godet flounce is very becoming to a full figure, as it tends to narrow the hips. ;„; ,

To my mind, the chief fault of dress, at present, from an artistic point of view, is the exaggerated pouching of the bodice in front at the waist. This gives a very ugly line to the figure, and more par- ticularly when the legs are short and the body long. When the pouched front is carried out in moderation it is not objectionable, but the aim of some of our dressmakers seems to be to disteLd the drooping folds of the over-lapping material, ballooning them outwards. Voile and canvas at now the favouride materials for dresses, and, as u rule, much elaboration is bestowed upon th, dresses made of them. Though nothing look, better or is more becoming than a plainly co, skirt with a shaped flounce, there are all sorts of strappings, tuckings, and other additions which do cot make the dress either more becoming or more durable, only more costly. On one skin only there are 37 strappings of silk running the whole way round. Another has 30 small tucks or pipings on the flounce alone, and several above it in groups of five. All this elaboration is so much pure waste of human energy, since it serves us good purpose.

The M 4-1 ;n hairdressing has not altered very‘ decidedly, yet many women who have a reputation for smartness are wearing their hair quite low, coiling it in a loose knot right at the nape of the. neck. This style, however, is best adopted in the evening only, as it does not look well under a hat; moreover, the all prevailing ruffle is apt to rub the coil into a deplorable state of untidiness. The front hair is always slightly waved, and is either rolled back over a small circular pad or frame (the large onas have had their day), or parted at the side with the curious curl, or rather large wave, in ••• the centre of the forehead. Fancy pins and combs hava gone considerably out of fashion for day- time wear, but all sorts of pretty ornaments are seen in evening coiffures. Little lace wings, wired to stand ap well ; cut jet and paste aigrettes, and small chaplets of leaves and tiny flowers, may be noted among the favourite hair.ornaments. Siv-irt sac coats in pique and coarse linens are being prepared for morning and seaside wear as the weather grows warmer, whilst long coat of the same will be worn for motor-car driving, and at some of the more-business-like race meetings. For the present faced cloth and r.ugh-surfaced tweeds are made up into long alsters, with loose double-breasted fronts, full backs, strapped in at the back, and large full hoods, lined with silk. Plerty of capacious pockets find titeir way into thes. accommodating sisters, for the benefit of- usually pocketless womankind, and one thoughtful tailor is putting a loose change and ticket pocket " into the broad cuff-band on the left-hand wrist, the cuff buttoning over, and making all secure, yet My of access.
Your loving JENrrnr.

Norway is scarcely the country where one would ex- pect to fir d emancipated woman in all her highest glory. The modernised woman, we all thought. WAS the pro- duct of the more progressivf cr.untries of the West, yet. as a matter of f-c', it is the,Norwegian women who are leading the way towards equalising the sexes. Many offices in the S' ate D-pertfnertahave beer opened up to them, while women paying taxes, or bolding property, are to have the franchiYe equally with men. Still more striking, as retards the a dvatcsment of women, is the recent act of the Legislatute.which enacts that the vow of obedience made by the wife in the marriage setvice, is henceforth to be optional. Such a half-way measure will strike many as being a mistake, as, whatever may he one's opinions on the sulject, clearly 'the present form should either he retained or. abolished. It is hardly a matter which should be leftlto couples to settle he'w een thernrelvea, as, in that case, one can easily imagine how that option may prove an element of -discord, and per- haps be the means of wrecking III&As ,Sarah Bernh a rdt, like Max O'Rell,lns been telling her people at home how much better the, American women are compired with their French s'sters.. Mani, B, rn- harrit'As a great Trans-Atlantic traveller, and sbe. ought to know, though one would think that her outspoken opinions will scarcely increase her popularity With the fair Parisians. The independence and intellectual superiority of the American women are the twr qualities which seem to fill these distinguished critics with ad- miration, and thie, on dnwhis trecanse th ---abenhlte freedom and self-reliance or the American Ori, is in such striking contrast with the restrictions which especially surround Frenchwomen. But all the world is moving in the same war, and if the divine Sarah will have A little patience, she- will probably live 'o sea ben countrywomen a great deal more emancipated than they are. div.p: STOCKTON HEATH PAROCHIAL
COMMITTEE.
."7 Interested Members and a yoestion of
Honour.

A meeting' of the Stockton Reath Parochial Com- mittee was held in the National Schoolroom on Thurs- day last week. Mr Clarke presided, and there were also present : Messrs Mclntyre, Pilling, Whitley, Fairhurst, Pemberton and Pearson, with G F Ashton (clerk), Far- rington (nuisance inspector), and Swinton (surveyor). PROPOSED IMPROVEMENT IN IVIUTEFIELD ROAD . . -

The committee resolved to ask the Runcorn Rural Districr Council to offer the sum of £3 to Mr Williams for a piece ot land to be acquired for the purpose of an improvement in Whitefield-road. The surveyor was instructed to prepare a tracing of the priposed improve- ment

TO PREVENT THE FLOODING Or FOOTPATHS The Clerk read the following communication Which be had reeeived from the assistant secretary to the Local Government Board :—I am directed by the Local Government Board to advert to your letter of the Bth inst. applying rn behalf of the Rural District Council of Runcorn for the istue of an order declaring section 74 of the Towns Improvement Clauses Act,1847,t0 be in force in the parish of Stockton Heath and lam to request that the Board may be furnishrd with a statement of the giounds upon v bich the application is made." The Clerk was instructed ,to write to the Lent oeveynnaent"l3oard informing them of these facts
. - THE CONSIDERATION OP PLANS-INTERESTED MEMBERS TO
REITIltli.

Mr Whitley proposed "That any person who may be a member of thia Parochial Committee, having plans for buildings or alterations before the meeting, shall retire whilst the same are beine considered by The Building Cornmittee and the Parochial Committee.'

- Mr Pemb:rton asked if the resolution,-when passed could be legally enforced. The Clerk replied that it could be enforced as regarded the Building Committee, bGt he did not think that meetings of the Parochial Committee they could refuse- to allow any member to remain in the room. He had a right to be there, and it was simply a question of honour as to whether be would refuse to retire.

Mr Whitley said he had been told by members of the committee that when the parties Concerted were present, the other members did not care to speak Be freely on the plans aa they otherwise would do. He thought that in common Courtesy the members interest- ed should retire.

Mr Mclntyre : I think it is rather .a reflection on the members of the committee who bappen to be presenting plans. Mr. Pilling : It is rather a de:icate question. Mr Mclntyre: Tau don't mean co say that any mem,. bar of the committee presenting plans takes advantage of his position 2= _

Mr Pilling: I do not wish to say so. You can please yourself what you think. Mr Whitley : I don't mean to pass any reil-ction on the committee but there are members who would net speak as freely as they would if the members would retire. The Chairman rem .rke,.l that a similar resolution had been passed previously. Mr Pilling said it was desirous that members should not adjudb•ate on their own plans. It was not fair. As to leaving it to their honour, he would not do such a thing. Be seconded the resolution. Mr Pemberton : I do not think that since I have been on the committee any member has voted on his awn-plans, Mr Whitley said that members had spoken upon their own plans. , Mr Pearson suggested that the resolution be amended to refer Only to the Building. Committee. As it hap— pened, the builderri - referred to were members of the committee.
4-emgw

The Chairman thought it.should also include the lay- ingtout of streets. Ultimately Mr Whitley altered his resolution to read las follows :—" That any person who May be a mem- ,l;ter.Af the Parochial Committee, having plans (includ- ing buildings or streets) before the meeting sball retire whilst the same are being considered by the Building Committee?

The reiklution tr,s unanimously adopted. skAttorirrirt noun To BE ERECTED.—THE CHAIRMAN'S The following letter was reau from Dr Adams, the Medical. Officer of Health, wish reference to a slaughter house proposed ty be erected at the rear of Haskell- -841,33 bf• Mr J Bailey. " I have considered the plans fora slaughter house for Mr J Bailey, proposed to be erected at S ekton Heath and am of opinion that if its use is strictis, restricted to ths number of animals proposed and if it is not let to other persona for ilsughtering persons, no nuisance can arise, and that Use,-cmunaittee. ,may recommend the plans to be sancioned." The Chairman: I think we should be doing a wrong' thing to the Community in allowing a slaughter house to be built in that position. If it is built there it may be a standing reproach tu us for years to come. The Inspector said Mr Bailey conferred with him in the first instance and he (Mr Farrington) did not give him any encouragement. Be bad had conversations with him several times since and he found he would have no objections to the committee granting the licence provisionally. They could grant the licence for not less than twelve months and it would have to be renewed. Mr Bailey was called into the room and guestionedby the chairman with reference to his specification. In answer to questions Mr Bailey said the animals would be killed in the morning about o'clock or between 9 and 12 when the children were in school. He would unOertake not to let the slaughter-house to any- one else. The refuse would be taken away twice a week.

It watt decided to grant a licence prcvisionally. The Chairman was the only member to vote against it, remarking tnat his conscience would not allow him to agree to the granting of the licence. This was all the business.

div.head: BOY DROWNED IN THE WESTON
div.p: BOY DROWNED IN THE WESTON
CANAL.
Gallant Attempt at Rescue.

-Coroner R 134)loson, held an inquest at the Royal Oak, Weston, on Monday night, which disclosed the lamen- table manner in which Harry Bonkem, aged 14 years, son of Mr Henry Bonkem, of 9, Salisbury-street, Run- corn, met his death.—lt appeared that Sunkem, in company with Cecil Speed,and Arthur &ugh, two lads of about the same age, and who resided with their parents in Shaw-etreet, Runcorn, went to bathe in the Weston Canal near liough's Bridge, on the previous Stturday afternoon. Speed and Bonkern got into the water about 2.30, and tfae former swam out to the pillar of the swing bridge. Ronkem followed,and Speed seeing that the effort would he too much for him called him to go back. Bonkem replied he would not. Speed then swam out to him, aad shouted to a man on the bank who went for a life belt. Speed tried to rescue Bonkem, but was dragged lunder water by him and had to let go. He then swam ashore ; and Bonkem was drowned before the man returned with the life-belt., Arthur Hough, the other lad, witnessed the sad catastrophe, but as be was but a poor swimmer could render no aid., Subsequently the body was recovered by Mr John William Norton, of Company's Rew, Wester], the deceased's uncle.—The Cu-oner highly complimented the boy Speed for his noble attempt at rescue. In summing up, be advised Ithe return of is verdict of " Accidentally drowted whilst bathing." lit. night say that last year there was not a single case of suen a death recorded within the Coroner. ship. Remarking on the want of proper bathing accom- modation for the youths of the district, Mr D ,bson said it seemed to him that .Runcorn was a place Of snffiaient largeness and importance to provide its inhabitants with swimming baths. Al there was no provision for boys they would fled somewhere to b +the, and the pity was they were obliged to bathe in paces mnre or less dangerous H • did not know the fe-ling in It tricorn with regard to public baths, but if th- authorities were disinclined to move in the matter, It mieht be that som wealthy philanthropist would u'timately provide what would be a very great boon not only to the young people, but to every one in Runcorn. (Cheers ) A verdict of droWned lotthing was returned. - - • • ,

tidy antage in a very cowardly way of the Council's cor- p ore te capacity he could tell them that they would 10 ave 'heard something from him (Councillor—F-14 R o rts). He bad been on the very point of challenging these gentlemen to charge him (CounCilkir 'Roberts) with the very thing which thy bad charged the Cor- poration with. If instead of saying the Corporation of Werrington were guilty of these abominable things, they bad said you (Councillor F R Roberts) are guilty of them, well he would have made a very good thing out of it. (Laughter.) The Corporation had acted with great dignity. There bad been no conspiracy of silence because there was nothing to conceal. He had been asked again and again by ratepayers whether there was anything in these abominable charees, and he had said there was nothing in them. He had also been asked the question " Are you in league together to keep the truth from us ? "and:his (Councillor Roberts') answer had been " I have been for four years a mem- ' ber of the Corporation and Final:ice Committee, and I can honestly say I know nothing whatever. ' Their silence had been entirely due to the conscious- ness that they were honourable, true and righteous men. (Hear, hear.) There was just enough in these charges to put them on their guard, and he thought the moral they ought to derive was that the verdict was "Not guilty ; but don't 'do it again." (Hear, hear). They bad done nothing except this, that they had put in the mouths of babes and sucklings (he was not referring to the Investigation Committee) tasty little bits which they had liked very much indeed but which unfor- tunately had been too small to permit of contin- uous enjoyment. He sincerely hoped that the gentlemen whe were concerned with this agitation against the Cor- poration, when they had paid the little bill of costs which tney had incurred in two unsuccessful actions against the Corporation, they would be content to let it rest and be satisfied that the Corporation was not the sink of iniquity which they would make the ratepayers believe: (Hear, bear.) Councillor Greening congratulated the sub-committee union their report, and also defended the action of the auditors. He remarked that the auditors were per- fectly juritified In pointing out these supposed irregu- larities. He took exception to what Councillor Tinnion had said as to Councillor Jolley having signed some of the orders in his capacity as a member of the Finance Committee, and argued that such a statement in regard to the etagere's auditor was very unfair. The MAYOR said bethought Councillor Greening was entirely labouring under a misapprehension as to what Councillor Tinnion intended to convey. Councillor TnesioN considered it only fair to himself that at this stage he should be allowed to make an ex- planation. What he said regarding Councillor Jolley actually formed part of the committee's report up to tte previous evening. They, however, had another meeting at ten o'clock that morning to reconsider the matter. They were agreed, and decided that the action of the auditors was to be commended, and that it was justified. They also considered that the action which the auditors had taken was in the interests of the borough, and, therefore, they took out of the report the paragraph relating to Councillor Jolley which he (the speaker) had read to the Council, and to which he thought Councillor Greening took exception. Their only reason for erasing it from the report was because they thought it might be construed by some as being un- favourable to the auditors. At the same time he con sidered it only right for him to bay e drawn attention t it, in order to show that members of the Council were not open to the charge which had been freely circulated concerning them. The committe.e recognized that in pre- senting their report they were dealing with a larger circle than the Warrington Corporation. It was a matter which concerned the whole of the ratepayers,and consequently, his colleagues and himself felt it only right and proper on their part to explain, on behalf of the other members of the Council, that even a gentleman like Councillor A .7 Jolley, whom he (Councillor Tinnion) considered to be one of the most enlightened and intelligent members of the Council, should sign orders for payment on tho Borough Treasurer. His point was, that if Councillor A J Jolley, a gentleman of such standing and position, signed these orders, it was only to be expected that other members of the Council with less knowledge and less ability than he might easily fall into the dame error. It was not until be became Mayor's auditor, with hii fuller information, and more extensive know ledge, that these matters were open to question by him. Be hau not the slightest intention to find fault with the work of the auditors, far from it. But he wished to show the difficulties of the position by pointing out that as an ordinary member of the Finance Committee Coulicillor A J Jolley did not find these matters out, and it was only when he became Mayor's auditor that he discovered them. Councillor GREENING showed that the Finance Com- mittee were justified in passing the accounts in the form they were presented to them. He also thought that the auditors were entitled to make the comments they did with reference to it. Alderman BOLTON agreed that the auditors should bring everything to the front and keep nothing back. The Council might rest satisfied that for the future everything would be done straightforwardly and above board, and neither the ratepayers nor anybody else would have cause to complain. rue auditors and the sub-committee were entitled to the thanks of the Council for their services. Councillor A. .1 JOLLEY said Councillor Tinnion had wide a statement to the effect that he (Cocncelor Jolley) did not know these particular matters were pion& until he found them out in his capacity as *yore auditor. That was not quite correct. He appreciated the friendly tone of Councelor einnion's °Widow, and his too flattering remarks about himself, bet he- desired to make it clear to Councillor Tinnion tbet he was of opinion that these things were wrens: *bete they came before the Committ e, and it would be "Attila the knowledge of members of the committee that he objected to them at the time. It was not trus that be did not discover these things until be became May or's auditor, for he was fully cogniz int of them as a mem- ber of the Finance Committee. Councillor Robetts seemed disposed to minimise the gravity of the charges brought by the euditors. He submitted that any trans- action that even seemed to cast a doubt upon any of the members of the Council ought not to be called paltry, (Hear, hear.) He thought everybody would agree that the Committee approached their work in a proper spirit, and with a determination to do everything thet was right to all concerned. He would not dare to offer any criticism on their report. It would be bad policy for him to attempt to do so, for the simple reason that in effect the committee had confirmed everything which the auditors had sake Alderman Seniors said it would Pave a go,scl deal of time and unpleasantness if the ?mance Committee refused to sign any cheeles until they were perfectly satisfied that they were legal arid Proper charges to make. It was a very unfortunate thing that some members of the C iuticil should in ke it a practice of giving information to outsiders concerning toe work of uifferent committees, and that these Matters should be discussed in the newspapers before any cisesideration bad been given to them by the Council as a body. It had gone forth that certain members of the Council and servants of the public bad been guilty of very dis- hon ourable acts, and any uupleasantness of this kind could be avoided if in future the cemrnittee positively declined to sign any cheques About which there might be the least desist. Councillor Jemss EVANS said he SAW from the report of the committee that Mr Silk promised to produce to the committee the receipts given by him .to tie colliery proprietors for commission received by him in the trans section, but that be had failed to do so. In his opinion it would have been much more satisfactory to the Council and to the public generally if that receipt had been proJeced. It was true that Mr Siik had submitted an affidavit to the effect that all pron.; derived from the sale or the cannel belonged to and was received by him solely, but he (Mr Evans) and others would have looked upon the work of the committee as being more csmplete, and certainly, with far more pleasure upon the report if the committee had been able to say that the receipts given by Mr Silk to the colliery proprietors , were produced for their inspection. It would then have ' shown to the ratepayers beyond all doubt that Alder- man Francomb had nothing whatever to do with the matter, and that it was purely a matter of business be tween the gas engineer, Mr Silk, and the colliery pro- prietors. The whole thing would then have been complete, Councillor WiertiNses asked if Mr Silk bought this cannel from the colliery company, could he not produce his receipts for the money that he Paid them The MAYOR observed that if it was a sale on com- mission Mr Silk would not have that evidence. The committee, however, had received a letter from the colliery proprietors, Messrs J and it Stone, substan- tiating the statement which Mr Silk made. and Mr Silk also made an affidavit to the same effect. Be could hardly suppose that a firm like Messrs Stone, men of considerable eminence, would lend themselves deliber- ately to a fraud upon this Council by sending a letter which contained a falsehood. (Hear, hear). Councillor WILKINSON raid he had to meet the obser- vations of certain ratepayers and he was unable to do so unless the whole case was complete. ChUnCillOT JAMES EVANS : (did not wish to create difficulties. The MAYOR I don't say you did. lam only stating that the letter was produced at the committee. Councillor JAMES Everts then inquired by whom the receipt held by the Corporation was signed. Councillor flexion : The report distinctly states that the cheques were made payable to Mr Silk, that they were endorsed by him, and paid into Mr Fran- comb's banking account. He repeated that the com- mittee had given this matter their most careful and serious consideration, and had given their decision upon the full evidei ee placed before them. With regard so the ques ion affecting Mr Silk they had his sworn affi- davit, and in addition they had a letter from the 3clliery proprietors Me isrs J and R Stone, r f Liverpool in which they said " The work was done by Mr Silk, who was allowed to put on commission for his services." With regard to Alderman Shaw Green, he acted for Mr James Parr and not on behalf of the Corporation. Mr Parr wrote in answer to a letter from the Town Clerk that Alderman Shaw Green had his express instructions to arrange the exchange. The committee was prepared in any el these matters to give any further information that might be required by any member of the Corpora-

He would say in conclusion that with regard to the wholesale slanders which had been made outside the Corporation, he woind commend to the people of Warringtou an epigram at the late George Elliott's. With regard to some ed these peopl they belonged to a class described;by George &Hat ai'people who christen private grudges by the name of public zeal." (Hear, hear.) Highland Malt Whisky is a simple distillation from Malt,made from Barley caret ull y dried in the Malt Kiln, and partakes, therefore, of the pleasant flaVoUr peculiar to dried Malt. The finest B srley. only 11 used, and ia its purchase keen competition always exists. Considerable quantities of cheap Grain Spirit are roads from Maize, foreign Barley and linmalted Grain, which, on account of their lower price,are used to blend with liMalt Whisky in order to produce a cheaper article. Without wishing to disparage the merits of Grain Spirit, it is not" Highland Malt Whisky," and W k A Gilbey maintain that such a blend should stand by itself and be sold under its proper designation of Grain Spirit. The public, with knowledge and taste, having Once appreciated the flavour of a Malt Whisky, will not find anything in blends composed partly of Grain Spirit to recommend them. W k A Gilbey, holding these views with regard to the higher merits of Highland Wnisky distilled only from the best of Malt, have used nothing else in the brands offered by them to the public for the past 40 years, and at both their own nistiVeries. which are situated in the best Barley districts ot Scotland—viz. " Glen-Spey " and " Strathoodi "I—their Whiskies are made entirely from Malted Barley grown in the _United Kingdom. W ik A Gilbey have 12,000 Butts of Scotch Whisky maturing in His Majesty's Bonded Warehouses, equal to , over 1,800,000 palrms at proof streng'h. and are thus etiabled by their large stocksto o. siotatu a thoroughly matured article, di.tiPers from par.. What we consider the best and cleverest verses will be awarded prises as above in their respective order of merit. The verses must be sent, post paid, on or be- fore 30th May, 1901, and accompanied by a receipt for something aced for spring cleaning, bought at any of the branches of BOOTS, Cash Chemists. You will get a receipt for everything you buy at the shops Of BOOTS, Cash Chemists.
The verses to become the property of BOOTS. Cash Chemists. for publication it desired, but the sender's name will not be published without permission.
Two or more sets of verses will be accepted from one sender, but each set must be accompanied by a separate receipt.
Prizes will not be awarded to employees of the firm.

_Urers• This leaves • the much wider question *Pen for consideration, how manufacture from Pure materials can be ensured ? Legislation may dO something, and perhaps it ought to be insisted on because it is remarkable that althoughtthe liquor trade is not subject to the stress of cempe- Won from which other trades suffer, and the pro- made continue to be abnormally large, these !sets have not prevented brewers from sacrificing the public safety for the sake If effecting a saving the cost of manufacture. Perhaps a more elfectual remedy may be found in the direction Pointed out by Lord GREY'S Public House Trusts, 'where the trade of public refreshment will be carried on in public interest and not for private Profit.

THE lines upon EaH Grey's Public which the Earl GREY'S House Trust Public House Reform taoVement proceeds are such as must commend it to all who grasp the facts and nocessities of the Present situation. The net profits from Public Uouses and Beershops in the United Kingdom for 1899 were estimated on good authority to amount to close upon twenty millions. Not only ticses this immense sum find its way into private hands bat it represents a huge and growing inter- cat, organised for trade and political purposes as Perhaps no other interest is organised, and )laving a most sinister effect on the social and Political body corporate. The Public House Trott (foes not propose to attack or supplant it; but it Proposes to work steadily and gradually towards decreasing its influence, gathering in the stray "rrents that are still left in free play in its sphere of action and setting up as a modifying influence higher regard for the public interest in matters Pertaining to the licensing of public places of refreshment. It will be the object of the Com- a to acquire every new License which the Licensing Authorities may think it desirable to create, and to apply to the Public Houses so acquired, and to existing Public Houses when ever it is possible to take over these, their principle of administration which will secure that they shall be managed as a Trust in the interests of the com- lamaftY, and not for private profit. Under the Present system, especially where "tied houses" exist there anis no security that the best liquor that Cbe bought in the open market is supplied, while it is the interest of the publican to push the Sale of the liquor he supplies. The method adopted to meet these two undoubted evils is to see that the liquor supplied by the Trust Houses is the hest that can be obtained in the open market; and to place the managers of the houses on a fixed salary, with commision only on the sale of food and non-intoxicants, or a bonus on good management. The Trust Houses will not be more drinking bars; they will be refreshment houses, in the fullest sense of the word, supplying well-served meals and what are designated temperance refreshments as readily as intoxicants. Interest not exceeding ..ve per cent, will be paid to shareholders, and after a sum has been laid aside for a reserve fund the remaining profits will be handed over to Trus- tees specially appointed to be administered by :hem in the interest of the community. The ob- 4ects to which these funds may be devoted will be l'clected by the trustees from the various objects utility which may be of interest to the . . es tr which the houses ate situated. They IV be used to establish libraries, read- -111g-rooms, clubs, recreation halls and grounds, an galleries and museums or any object 'Which may . serve as a counter-attraction to the public-house, and which the local authorities do not find means at their disposal to provide. They may be used in whole or in part for the pur- Pose of buying up licenses with the view either of administering them on the companies' principles or suppressing them altogether, where it is found they are not required. The great possibilities which the last-named alternative opens up are of themselves an important recommendation to the Scheme. A way is thus suggested whereby, when a alglicient redemption fund had been formed, a corn- InUnity might not only reduce the number of its PUblic-houses, but by a vote of the inhabitants Qatinguisl, them entirely, without being called upon to pay any compensation to anyone. The IClMvement is one which commends itself to Philanthropists, to all who lay claim to public aPint, and to every practical reformer on temper- ance lines who desires to see some progress made towards the elimination of the evils of the drink

THE great English race- Derby Day. meeting has come and gone; and it has left re- flections. A holiday usually does bring reflections. If it has been well spent, these are of a pleasant character and go to increase the store of happy Memories which one likes to recall. There are holidays however which do not leave a pleasant taste in the mouth, and it is to be feared that the great majority of those who found their pleasure at Epsom on Wednesday will return to their tegular occupations sadder though not neces- eerily wiser men. Horse-racing in itself is a legitimate sport; and the Anglo - Saxon taco are devoted sportsmen. But the excitement attendant on its practice has drawn to it so many aasociated evils that it is difficult to justify even a tiessic event like the Darby as at present carried °lit. The associations of dissipation, gambling, t°guery and the meanest kinds of vice which clus- ter around it quite outweigh any advantages which tall be urged in its favour. The vice of gambling alone has increased to such an alarming extent 111 the country, that every incentive to its propaga- tion must be viewed with the strongest suspicion 133? all lovers of their kind. It is one of the saddest things about horse-racing that it is only in very „,arel cases that it is engaged in for pure love of.sport. -Lnieed the great race meetings could not be tarried on if there were not added to the legiti- b,aate interest of the races that more sordid but !teener interest involved in having" a bit on." It 1,5 only too true that the same avaricious spirit has become associated with all kinds of sports and "the betting " has become the great feature of inter- net in all the great sporting events which ill °or newspapers, from a prize-fight to a yacht- taco- It is true that the same tendency may be °hserved in business, where speculation has largely taken the place of sober trade ca. lculations,and the results, as frequently revealed bathe bankruptcy and criminal courts, cannot be ct/ hternplated with any degree of satisfaction. It i a pity that an abnormal greed of gain should tesnit f torn the uncontrolled pursuit of business; but under the stress and strain which characterise 7,odern trade it is at least natural. It is a sadder Pity still that the recreations of the people which °I:II:gilt to lift them out of the sordid atmosphere 11100eY-gettiog only-plunges them ideeper in the "u!st avarice. The healthy relaxation, which

ought to tone 'up and stimulate body and rrind for undertaking afresh the duties of life, is being supplanted by the gambler's curse which eats out the heart, body and soul of all classes of oar people, and threatens national de* generacy if a better tendency does not soon set in. Perhaps the worst case is that of those who having to remain at work on Derby day seek to beguile the tedium of their occupation by backing their favouritie3 or taking a draw in the inmocent looking sweep-stake. The energy that might bring a good return if devoted to the work in hand is thus frittered away in puerile excitement over the chance of making a "pot" by the risk of a smaller sum. The principle is essentially immoral' because the transaction benefits no one There is no pretence even of rendering an equiva- lent for the value received. What one gets another or it may-be many (Alters lose. Even the winner is not benefited, because his " luck " induces only a more reckless spirit of speculation which leads him to tempt fate until inevitable disaster, it may be ruin, finally overtakes him. The evil is so wide-spread that it is to be feared little can be done by cheese-paring restrictions. So long as the present materialistic outlook is maintained in matters of business and pleasure, the people will take both in their own way. The only " way out" is a higher moral and spiritual tone. When the country in its need seeks for deliverance, then it shall find it.

Lord Milner, it is probable, will not go to the expense, at present at all events, of purchasing a set of scarlet and ermine robes for his formal introduction, as these would be useless to him for a very long time to come, in view of his early return to the Cape. What the High Com- missioner will most likely do will be to borrow from some accommodating peer the necessary paraphernalia, and armed with these he will make the quaint perambulation of the Chamber in the course of a few days. A great deal of nonsense has been written as to the. alleged celerity with which his lordship's patent is being prepared. Is a matter of fact, these are always kept in stock at the Crown Office, so that it is only necessary to fill in the name add description of the new peer and to get the Sovereign and the Home Socretary for the time being to affix their signatures at the top and bottom respectively. In like manner the which are green, red, blue, large waxen seals, yellow or white, according to .the rank of the prospective peer, are also kept in stock, and have merely, when the time comes, to be heated and stamped with the Great Seal.

The 21st annual report of Dr Gornall on the health of Warrington for the year 1900 is not one upon which we can justly flatter ourselves. The death-rate (194 per thousand of population) we i are told, is higher than t has been of late, though lower than the average of the past ten years. From the table of statistics showing the death-rate in other towns, Warrington seems to occupy a middle position. There are many towns with a death-rate lower than Warrington whilst on the other hand there are others with a higher rate. For instance, one almost envies Northampton of its low death-rate of 131 per thousand as com- pared with 19.4 in Warrington, but this last- named figure is much more satisfactory than Bootle's 22.7, or our nearer neighbours, Wigan, where the death-rate is 21.9. In the birth-rate statistics Warrington holds a much stronger posi- tion and comes out near the top with a birth-rate of 361 per thousand. This leads the Medical Officer, whom we are sure everyone will regret to hear is incapacitated from following his duties at present, to make a few interesting remarks on the factors which lead up to such a result. Not much satisfaction can be gained from a perusal of Dr. Gornall'a black list of insanitary dwelling- houses. Scores of houses which have been reported as insanitary are still unattended to, and in this respect the members of the Corporation lay themselves open to censure. It is useless asking the Medical Officer of Health for a list of insani- tary properties, if no steps are to be taken to force the owners to make them habitable, and it is idle to suppose that Warringtan will ever have a low death rate so long as people are allowed to live under such conditions.

An inquiry is to be hold on Friday the 14th inst. into the application of the Corporation for sanction to borrow £7,000 for extensions at the baths. Half this sum is required for the erection of Tutkish baths as an adjunct to the plunge and wash baths now existing. Would it not be advisable, in view of the present high rates, to postpone this portion of the scheme for, say, three years? We have never looked with favour on the idea of spending ' £3,000, or more, on Turkish baths in Warrington, and there is plenty of opposition in the town to what appears very much like unjustifiable expendi- ture. The workingmen do not want such luxuries at so great a cost, and we have never yet seen evidence of the demand which is going to make the scheme pay according to those members who wear rose-coloured spectacles and who, by the way, are users of the Turkish bath themselves. The scheme is not froe from the suspicion of sel- fishness, and it would be a source of gratification to us to see some of our more public-spirited townsmen protesting at the inquiry against this part of the proposed extension. Economy in all things must be the watchword if our rates are ever to come down to a normal level.

It would indeed have been remarkable if the present spell of hot weather had run its course ere we were reminded of the foul smells emitted from Sankey Brook. At the meeting of the Great Sankey Parish Council last week there were no fewer than four strongly-worded com- plaints from well-known gentlemen respecting this filthy stream. In dry weather when no fresh water eaters the brook it is practically an open sewer from St Helens to Sankey Bridges; and it is not surprising that Colonel Ridgway should warn the authorities of a probable epidemic of diphtheria. It is .surprising that they are so quies- cent in the face of so grave a daager. The people of Warrington were given to understand that the Corporation of St Helens had at length been compelled to take steps to prevent the pollution of the stream, but we have heard very little of this lately and there is cer- tainly no perceptible improvement in the con- dition of ,the Brook. in fact it can never have been worse than it is at present. It is high time that the Local Government Board stepped in and called upon the St. Helens Corporation and any other authority guilty of polluting the brook, to stop!

div.head: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
div.p: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
A Provincial Letter.
disco,

Inasmuch as a little experience is of more value than much theory, those who believe that good may result from public-house reform should feel interested in the " remarkable results" claimed for experiments which have been carried on in Scot- land. Branches of the public-house trusts have been formed in several of the towns beyond the border. In two of them public-houses have been worked on the Gothenburg system for a sufficiently long time to demonstrate the advantages which this plan possesses over public-houses conducted for private gain. Hill-of-Beath has had its reformed public-house since June, 1896. Its population of 1,300 is apparently by no means composed ot tee- totalers In the first four month 4 the receipts were £516, and in nine months ended December last,had reached £2,156. B it if the people drank a good deal they had something in return, Out of the profits the village has been lighted by electricity a bowling-green has been hid out,and an institute, lcomprising reading-room, library, billiard-room I etc, has been established. In Kelty, another small place, a lious • was opened in Ainuary, 1900, and although there were six otheF licensed houses there, the CiJtlienburg system found immediate

favour, and with similar results as far as they have gone. A village library hag been formed, and a district nurse appointed. It is, perhaps, not quite right to say that these places are eating and drink- ing themselves into a condition of comfort unknown to their neighbours, but the exaliples serve to show that if there must be public-houses it is better that they should be conducted for the public benefit than for the private gain of those whose one interest is to sell as much drink as possible.

At Tunbridge Wells on Saturday a proposition was laid before a meeting of traders for the estab- lishment of a regular system of motor trains be- tween that town and London. The reason assigned for such action is the unsatisfactory attitude of the railway company towards the local goods traffic. One of the results, of course, has been to draw the attention of those whom it may concern in other towns similarly situated, to the fact that no parliamentary powers are required for the run- ning of so-called "motor-trains. Hence the possi- bilities are that the Tunbridge Wells experiment may prove to be the pioneer of important systems of locomotion, both within and without ary given urban district, inasmuch as the developments can be carried a long way without the aid of coal. But successful competition with railway companies is another question.

For the consolation of newspaoer readers who may have been led by recent prognostications as to the forthcoming failure of our British coalfields, and suggestions as to what we may be expected to do after that happens, it may be mentioned that the latest evidence of enormous supplies of mineral oil being available throughout the world, comes to us in the shape of what is called"the Texan boom." The truth is that petroleum wells of tremendous yielding power, and easily accessible, have been Aiscovered at Beaumont, in Texas. There is no reason to anticipate that this discovery will revolutionise the oil-market of the world, because the Texas oil-yield will be controlled by the gigan- tic American trust which dictates prices and regu- lates transactions. The peculiarityof the oil raised at Beaumont, however, is that, according to the "Board of Trade Journal," it is capable of being produced ant marketed at a minimum cost. As the official report sets forth, the oil is being produced within eighteen miles of a seaport, can be piped into tank steamers at a cost so small as to be almost incalculable, and P can be delivered at the seaports of the United States, Mexico, the West Indies, South America, and Europe at a cost so low that no other fuel can be used in competition against it for steam purposes. As, according to the Government report of 1899, the average cost of coal exported from the United States was 268 dollars (its 2d) per ton, it is readily seen that it is really d not a ques- tion of competition, but rather a question of profit." This is the official statement, and is so extraordin- ary that it cannot fail to arrest the attention of the coal consuming world, which, if it were enabled to participate in it to the full, would be constrained to regard it as epoch-making not only in relation to marine traffic, but in connection with factories and railways. At present the question is whether the United States will care to admit the outside world to a full participation in its wealth of liquid fuel. But if it did uot, it might still make an enormous profit out of the Texan oil-yield, and yet he: able to supply the world's demands at a, price that would, of many purposes, exclude steam coal from the market altogether. Than the people can do in England, as has been done for generations in parts of Wales, utilise the small coal for moulding into briquettes.

Only two of the men who lost their lives in the Sengbenydd colliery disaster last week were members of the Miners' Permanent Provident Society of South Wales. As showing the clangorous character of coal mining and the necessity which exists for a fund of this kind, it may be stated that during the past three months thirty men received fatal injuries, and their representatives drew their money from the Society. The old age alhwance movement is making due progreas among them, seventy-five men having recently been added to the number of pensioners, tnus bringing the total num- ber in receipt of a weekly allowance:of five shillings to 187. So far as its members are concerned, the Society may be said to have practically solved the old age pengion problem—at any rate, to their own satisfaction, and it would be well if many other industries would do likewise.

The annual report of the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants, just published, derives a special interest from one or two particularly important facts. The first is that there are a couple of disputes in which it is taking part, namely the dismissal of the Great Eastern men, and the differences in oath Wales; and secondly, one of its own members has been returned to Parliament, for the first time in the history of the organisation. The S-miety has always taken a practical interest in legislation affecting railway servants, and Mr Bell M.P„ says that the report of the Royal Commission on Accidents, and the powers that will doubtless be given effect to in con- nection with dangerous railway operations, will mark a great step in the history of the society, An I organisation which does so mush to succour the orphans of devased members, and aims to make it pos.ible for railway servants to lead happier and healthier lives,certainly deserves all the encourage- ment •that can be given Ito it, and on the whole the report for the year is satisfactory. It shows that the membership continues to increase, having risen from 59,818 to 62,023. Although this Is a substantial total, however, it cannot be said that it is as large as it would be if the different grades of railway servants fully appreciated the benefits conferred by the society. Few trade or- ganizations are managed more judiciously than has been that of the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants, while during its existence the executive have done much to lesson or to prevent serious friction between the workers on the railways and their employers. There have been big strikes, but the executive have generally earned credit tor the way in which they have assisted in adjusting the differences that have arisen, and the public hope and expect that they will continue the same kind of policy.

div.head: AN INTERESTING FIUURE IN SOCIETY.
div.p: AN INTERESTING FIUURE IN SOCIETY.

One of the most popular members of Lindon society is Mrs De Vere Brookf;, who attained considerable celebrity as a society beauty, and whose capabilities as an elocutionist have often been revealed in amateur theatricals performed in high circles. She is a daughter of the la.e member for Dudley, who represented that division for over thirty years.

Mrs Do Yore Brook o spends bet leisure time at her Brighton residence, 8, Linadowne-square. Hove. "Yes," she told a "Weekly D:spatch" reporter the ether day, "the demands of society life fall heavy on a popu- lar favourite. lam always fully occupied with social enga s gements but about lour years ago I began to fear that I would have to give up, for I found out, for the first time in my life, what indigestion really meant, although previous to this, even the exacting fatigue of a heavy London season left me with nothing worse than a alight headache.

'I adopted many sumstions made by friends," Mrs De Vere Brooke continued, " and variouB remedies were tried without relief. But on one occasion, whilst, discussing the symptoms of indigefition with a lady friend of mine. I had my attention drawn to Dr. Williams' pink pills for pile people, and decided to try them. I carefully observed the instructions, an in less than a week I felt better. B.,fore I bad exhausted the contents of one box the indigestion had disappeared. and two boxes entirely cured me. Whenever I feel tired after my social engagements I know where to seek relief."

According to the "Suns" Dr. Williams' pink pills are a fashionable craze of the moment—a craze stimulated, no doubt, by persi,tmt rumour regarding the circum- stances in which they gained countenance and high approval in a certain foreign Royal family.

The world knows little of its greatest sufferers. Women beer in silence what would often send strong men to their beds: in no way have Dr. Williams' pink pills done more good than to women of all ages, from girlhood to age. They relieve the headaches, the agonis- ing backaches, the constant or regularly recurring pains and misery which curse so many live!: while to men they are an unf ailing tonic and nerve restorer, curing (in both sexes) anaemia, consumption, rheumatism, sciatica, St. Vitus' dance, paralysis, indigestion, bile, and loss of appetite and strength. For two shillings and ninepence (six boxes, thirteen and nine), Dr. Willienve medicine company, 11-ilborn Viaduct. div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
DEATH OF A WIDNES_ IRONIVIASTER.

Mr Th—ol—a-s—Ro-b-inson, founder of Robinson and Cook, iron founders, St. fielens,and Widnes Foundry Company, Widnes, died on Monday morning at the residence of his son, Mr Joseph Robinson, Farn- worth, following an apoplectic seizure last Friday. He was 87 years of age,and for 60 years had played an important part in the industrial life of South- west Lancashire. He was also a leading Wesleyen Methodist, and was highly respected in the district:

POOLE'S NEW MYRIORABIA. Messrs H and F Poole with the new Myriorama, will visit the Public Hall, Runcorn, on Monday next, June 10th, and will stay for six nights. The programme includes a series of pictures from Lon- don to Pretoria with "Bobs" and Buller, and nu- merous other pictures of stirring events In addi- tion there will be twelve "star" variety turns of an excellent order, and an excellent series of animated photographs shown by an expert operator. An orchestral band unner the direction of Mr GJ Yar- wood will render selections. Those who desire to see a good show, will do well to visit the Public I Hall, during this, Me=srs Poole's first visit. COLONEL WRIGHT AT RUNCORN. There was a fair attendance at the Citadel,High- street, on Sunday evening, when a stirring dis- course was delivered by Colonel Ted Wright, of the "S. A." Twenty years ago Colonel Wright, who is a native of Runcorn, was a" terror to the Army," now he is one of its most useful members. He has been to New Zealand and Japan, and is now stationed at Brighton:—On the Sunday afternoon, Colonel Wright addressed the members of the Bethesda P.S.A., who were assembled under the presidency of Mr S Pope, and was listened to by a large gathering.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn County Court on Tuesday his honour Judge Bowen Rowlan is gave his award in the arbitra,ion proceedings under the Workmen's Com- pensation Act 1897, between Edith Allen Massey, widow, of 48 Union-street, R moor°, and the Ship Canal Company. Mr F. A. Lake instructed by the Upper Mersey Watermen's Assoziation officiated for the claimant. It appeared that on April 6 h James Massey, husband of the claimant, who was a workman in the employ of the Company was killed at Liverpool Docks by the crate falling upon him. The Company ad- mitted their liability and were willing to pay into court as compensation £250 34 lid. The widow had five young children dependent upon her. The Judge ordered that £2B 3s 11d:be paid to the widow and that the balance be invested in the name of the registrar of the Court and paid to her in quarterly instalments at the rate of 15s per week. Casts were allowed against the Ship Canal Campany.

SAILORS AND POLWR Al WIDNES' Alfred Symonds, Maurice Matthews,Robert Price and trrneet Winning, sailors, were paid off a the ttuncorn Docks•on Friday. At night all were more or less under the influence of drink, and created a disturbance in Regent-street. Constable Joseph P. Gregory requested them to go quietly to thsir ships, but they u ed bad language and pointedly told the eonstable"they would not go,neither could be make them ; two sailors were as good as a policeman." A fracas enFued,and Gregory was obliged to whistle for assistance. Constables Bowyer, Gilpin, and a number of civilians appeared on the scene ; but it was not until Constables Gregory and Bowyer had been assaulted, and Constable Gilpin seriously obstructed in the discharge of his duty, that Messrs Bailey, Arden, Cooke, and Parker came to the assis- tance of the police, and the prisoners were secured. , The following morning Messrs F J Norman and E 'raison, J P's, fined Symonds .£3 16, or thirty-five days' hard labour; Winning, .£2 us or twinty-one days; Price, 26s 61 or 14 days; and Matthews Ils 6d or seven daos.—The civilians were accorded the thanks of the Court.

A CHAPTER. OF AMIDRNTS About noon on Sunday, William Henry Shep• herd, aged 12 of Wellington-strest, who was play- ing on the stage of the Ferry, tell into the shallow edge of the Ship Canal. He was, however, promptly rescued by Mr James Gresn, of Coopsr-street, who was attracted to the spot, and who went into the water without even divesting himself of any cloth- ing.—On Sunday evening, Mr Henry Evans, mana- ger of the milk department' of the Runcorn Co-op- erative Society, was following his usual duties at the stab'es when he fell through a trap door from one storey of the building to another. He alighted rather awkwardly on the corner of a box, and when later, he was examined by Dr McDougall, it was found that he had fractured ssveral ribs, and sus- tained scratches about the face. He is now pro- gressing as favourably as can be expected.—On Monday morning, a man named Robert Jones, aged 57 years. 24 Warrington-road, labourer at the Lan- cashire Metal Works. Widnes, was following his employment when he slipped over a brick and fractured the right leg. He was removed to the Accident Hospital and attended to by Dr Hutchin son. He is progressing favourably. RUNCORN SCISOOL BOARD. The monthly meeting of the Board was held at the Town Hall, last week, 1 here were present:— The Rev Canon Maitland Wood (chairman), Mr Imison (vies-chairman), and Messrs F J Norman. J Littler W J Cunningham, J W Lightburn (clerk), and A Lightburn (assistant clerk). The resignation of Miss Garner (mistress of the Granville-street School), was accepted with regret, and it was re- solved that Miss Robb be appointed head mistress of Granville-street School, at a salary of £430 per annum; and that Miss Mary Warburton, of War- rington Training C Mlege,bs appointed head teacher , at Mill Brow School at a salary of .£7O per annum ' The Clerk.submitted theastiMates for the half-year ending September 29 The The amount required from the rates was the saihe as that for the corres- ponding half of last year. Mr Imison thought the ratepayers would be pleased to see that they were asking for £5O less than they did last year, and also that they were providing quite sufficient to discharge all their liabilities, and to leave them with more money in band than they had at the corresponding period.

THE THEFT OF UNDERCLOTHING.

At the Runcorn Sessions on Monday,Lillie Draper aged 13 years, who was remanded on a charge of stealing a towel and various articles of underclothing from the house of Margaret Ellison, 45, Ashridge-st on the previous Wennesday, pleaded guilty.—The father agreed to the girl being sent to Miss Wrights home for girls at Chest,n., and to contribute 2s a week towards her maintenance there, on which understanding the Bench dismissed the case.
6' THE GRAND OLD MAN" OF RUNCORN WEELEYANISIL

Runcorn'Wesleyans have been delighted for some ' time with the prospects of a visit from Mr. John Simpson (their grand old man), and who. fer over half a century was connected with the Brunswick Sunday School, the close of his connection with which place was marked by a period of service as superintendent which established a record both for length and zealousness. Po Runcorn Wesleyans Mr Simpson is indeed an honoured head, and when his proposed visit was realised his movements were watched with considerable interest. On Sun- day he attended divine service at the St Paul's and Halton-road churches, and also visited Old Bruns- wick, the scene of his yeoman service in Sunday school work. Here he was accorded a tremendous reception. On Monday evening, the aged gentle- man attended the circuit sewing meeting at Bruns- wick, and received quite a host of friends who were formerly associated with him there. Among those present were the circuit ministers, viz., the Revs A Wells (superintendent), H Morrison, and J B Foster, Messrs F J Norman, J K Frith, H H Poe-. nett, J Mason Frith. T Simister and 11l Taylor (the present superintendents of Brunswick scholl). and a large number of lady workers. a brief adress Mr Simpson expressed his satisfaction and pleas- ure at being able to visit Runcorn once more and finding the work of the circuit in such good hands. He trusted Methodism would make greater strides in the future than it had done in the past. Mr Simpson has for the past two or three years ra- sided at Colwyn Bay:

div.head: SS.- RUNCORN NOTES. --- EBY A CORUESPONDRNT 1
div.p: SS.- RUNCORN NOTES. --- EBY A CORUESPONDRNT 1

The best way to break hard stones is to keep on hammering them, and the party in power in our local School B iard, recognising the fact, have been at work for the past three years, strengthening their position, and disposing of the stones as they came up. On the other hand the progressives have missed many opportunitie4,and instead of having a true educationalists already on their side, the party rests only upon the rick-bed of Nonconformity. If the School Board is to be won back, it is only to be done by a tremendous effmt—by an effort, which, if accomplished, will boa triumph for Non- conformity, and which will for all time secure accommodation for their children in Board not Voluntary Schools.
From a reliable, though unofficial, source, I learn the Transporter Bridge undertaking will be com- menced before the end of July.

The Runcorn Park and ir lake are a great source of delight, but there are evidences which show" that the model yachting isiikely to become a great nuisance, if not controlled in some way. Many townspeople are talking of it, hence I invite dis- cussion.

Referring to the Transporter Bridge at the Dis- trict Council meeting, Mr Imison illustrates the fact that the rosy view entertained by some of the keenest supporters of the Bridge Scheme, that the Council would be able to borrow the money at 31 per cent., has proved fallacious. I amongst others was one of the " keen3st " advocates, but the figures as worked out by the advocates of the Bridge ranged from n per cent, to nearly four per cent; and, it was shown, that even at the highest per centage the concern was likely to pay, and prove a beneficial investmhnt for the town.
On Sunday evening last the Wesleyans of th Runcorn circuit held the first of a series of open air meetings in Devonshire-square. The gathering was a large one and eminently satisfactory.

With regard to the Coroner's remarks concerning the need ef baths in Runcorn," our city fathers" are quite agreed. And in fairness to them it should be stated that for a considerable time past they have been expending their energies in the d'rection of a feasible and economic scheme to meet the case Be. fore long we shall probably have two baths, one in the vicinity of the Park and Common, awl one on the bank of the Ship Canal on the site (probably) of the old baths.

Another District Council meeting has gone by but there has been no indication given 114 that the Volunteer heroes of Runc-nm, are to receive a tangible evidence of their appreciation from the town. Why is this? True, many of us do not agree with war, but there is not a single one of us wno does not appreciate the efforts of the poor fellows that fight for us

The ordinary monthly meeting of this Council was held at the Town Flail, on Thursdal. Mr RII Poonett, J.P., presided, and there were also present Messrs W Handley,E unison, J P. CC, S Taylor J P. D Bisbrown, M J Sweetman, J 11 Salkeld, J W Lightturn, J Wilson, J Pritcherd, J P, 11 G Kirk- ham, E Gatley, S Walton, El J Once, F Wiswall, with Mr F A Lake (law clerk) Mr E Marshall (secretary), Mr J Willing (surveyor), and Dr F McDougall (medical officer.) A statement of the in-ome and expenditure of the Waterworks Department for the year ended March 31st, 1901, wivi presented. Mr Pritchard explained that in 1900, after allow- ling for the sum of £lBO 173 Bd, being id in the pound on the General and District Rate, levied to meet the extra expenditure on spat, there was a loss of £419 6s 71, wllich with the loss that year (2142 9s 81), totalled £561 16s 3d. The penny in the .£ for the yeir ended March 31st, 1901 produced £lB4, and reduced the loss up to date to £377 16s 3d. He considered it was a very satisfactory working account for the past twelve months especially so when they considered the exceptional circumstances. The minutes and report were unanimously agreed to.

div.head: TIM TIUNEIPOUTER BRIDGE.
div.p: TIM TIUNEIPOUTER BRIDGE.

Dealing with the Financial report, which in- cluded a recommendation, that " the Ecclesiastical Commissioners be asked to lend .ClO,OOO for thirty years at £3 12s 6d per cent. interest," Mr Imison explained it was to enable the Council, to meet the calls in respect of the shares to be subscribed under the Widnes and Runcorn Bridge Act, 1900. It was intended to repay the money by equal half-yearly instalments of principal and interest, subject to the Commissioners agreeing to lend the money in instalments over two years. He pro- posed the application be made, but wished to point out the tranqaction was the first evidence that the anticipations of those gentlemen who had so keenly advocated the investment in the Bridge, had proved to be a failure. It had been asserted, as an argument in favour of the investment, that the Council would be able to borrow the money at 3t per cent., but they were unable to do ao. The Council would be obliged to provide £552 5s 104, plus the procuration fees and stamp duties. Of course, it was unfortunate that the Council had been unable to secure better terms. He thought, however, it should mako the Council pause before entering into such investments in the future Be proposed the adoption of the report. Mr Salkeld seconded. Mr W Handley replying to Mr Imison, said it appeared as if Mr Imison stood as a pessimist, and himself colon optimist in their respective attitudes regarding the Bridge. Mr Imbon seemed to shut out altogether the benefit that would accrue to the town when the Bridge was accomplished. Subsequently the Financial report was adopted'

THE ISOLATION HOSPITAL QUESTION, The Local Government Board wrote under date 23 d May, enquiring as to the present position of the leo!a- -non Hospital question. Mr S Woodward reported that the Committee appoin- ted to consider the matter met on Thursday morning last, and visited the site approved by the Rural D strict Council, and in company with the agent of the Aston Estate went carefully over the ground. Thy considered it in every way adaptable t 3 the requirements of the Hospital. The meeting was then adjourned, and resurn. d that morning, when they had a neflnite proposal placed before them by the agent for the property. This was for the sal. of the piece of land including the woodland adjacent, in all about eight acres, for £1,050. The Committee after very carefully considering the matter, and in view of the fact that ultimately they would be bound to provide an Isolation Hospital for the Diatrict, unanimously recom-nended the purchase at th'e figure quoted, autij .0t to the approval of the Local Government Board, and to such drainage rights as might be required being granted.—He moved tie adoption of the report; and would move,at the next meeting, that the land he purehAsed. div.p: THE HAWSERS OF S-ALT SCALE.

Mr William Dunbavin, Old Hall Farm, Weston, writing on the 90. h of May, asked the Clerk to kindly bring before the Council the question of salt scale on the Weston roads. He thought it was injurious to the feet of cattle that had to travel three or four times a day upon it. List year two of his cows fell lame,and be believed the lameness was caused by the salt scale, as the foot of one of the cows was worn quite through. The Surveyor intimated that the complaint was the Ars he had ever received, although salt scale had been lonsiderably used for road material in the district. Mr Woodward and several other members were of Opinion that " chippings " were just as liable to cause cows to go lame. Mr Guest whilst admitting the usefulness of the salt scale as road material, thought perhaps the large dikes of the scale afforded an element of danger. Ultimately it was decided that the Surveyor make inquiries and report to the next meeting. MORRIS BROOK.

div.head: HISTORIANS IN CHESHIRE.
div.p: HISTORIANS IN CHESHIRE.
Oa Saturday afternoon good nurnbPr of members of the Lsncasbire and Cheshire Elis:orical Ssciety and

friends spent a pleasant aftromoon in an interestinq part of Cheshire. Toey travelled by train to Northwich, whence they were driven in convevances to Budworth. Mr W Handley of Runcorn, officiated as guide and Arley Hall and Great Bud worth Church were inspected. Mr Handley had written the following brief description for the information of the members whicl prayed highly useful. ARLEY HALL, ASTON BY BUDWORTH.

The township of Aston by Budworth has been the possession of the Warburton's since the reign of Henry 111. about 1216, and was purchased by Geoffrey. the son of A lam-de-Dutton, who assumed the name of War- burton from his adopted place of abode. Arley Hall, was built by Piers Warburton in the reign of Henry VII, 1485-1495. Until that date the family resided at Warburton. The original building was of wood and plaster surrounded by a moat. It remained in that state until altered by Sir Piers, the 4th Baronet about 1755-8 when the old hall was encased with brick It was almost :entirely rebuilt, 1833-1842 from designs by Latham in imitation of a Cheshire house of the period of James I. The hall forms a quadrangle 114 in front by 130 feet in depth enclosing a cowl; 60 feet by 40 feet laid out with parterres of flowers. A principal feature of the exterior is the central turret with projecting oriel enriched with sculptural and armorial designs by WU- lenient, executed by Thomas. Over the entrance door of the stately hall on the stone porch is carved the kindly invitation This gate is free to all good men and true, Right welcome thou if worthy to pass through." The South front contains the library, hall, and gallery The gallery is 60 feet long and is wainscotted with oak grown on the estate. The carved oak staircase occupies a considerable space. The drawing-room is situate on the east side overlooking the terrace garden. The dining•room, though much altered, was the old hall of the original timber mansion. The carved oak book- cases in the library are from designs by Hering. On the north side adjoining the house stands the chapel, built of Runcorn stone in 1845 from designs by Salvin. it was enlarged by the addition of a north aisle in 11556-7 by Street, and is capable of seating 200 persons ITo the west of the hall is an interesting relic of the Fifteenth Century, a long spacious barn, eo-eval with the original timber Iv.ume. Massive oaken beams, or rather trees, roughly hewn, spring from the ground, meet under the ridge of the roof and spanning the entire width of the building present a series of pointed arches. The sides, of strong framework, are filled in with very thick panels of split oak boards, which after having been exposed to the atmosphere for 400 years are as sound as when first fixed in their grooves. Among the archives is a curious rent roll of the time of Queen Elizabeth, composed of sheets of parchment stitched together and ornamented with a rich border: In the library is a choice collection of autograph letters of English poets. The pictures are chiefly family portraits, GREAT BUDWORTH CHURCH. The Church stands on a lofty knoll between Bud. worth Mere and Pickenere. Its situation gives it an ex- tremely handsome and imposing appearance. It was given to the Priory of Norton by William, Baron of Halton and Constable of Cheshire in the reign of Henry 1135. After the dissolution of the Monasteries by Henry VIII, the Rectories of Budworth and Runcorn were given by him to Christ Church, Oxford. The present Church dates from 1400-1432- On the left hand of the steeple door n-ar the bottom is the remains of an Inscription in ancient character. Argil's Egard, Vidue (Margaret Gerrard,widow) which probably commemor- ate her as a special benefactor in the construction of the steeple. Just over the steeple door under the great window are three coats of arms. On the left corner, the family of Dutton on the right corner, the Priory of Norton, in the middle—Warburton—en one ' side of which is written, John, on the other Warburton, Knight. On ether parts of the steeple and also on the walls of the Church are carvings which indicate restor- ation or addition about the end of the r ign of Henry VII. It is said that the organ in use at Norton Priory was removed to Budwortlo Churn but this gave place to a now one in the reign of Charles 11. The Interior of the Church underwent restoration in 1269 and the unsightly galleries of the north aisle and at the west end were tatren down On the sides of the chancel are ten ancient carved oak stalls with subsellia• The South Transept is a chancel exclusively devoted to the Warburtons of Arley. On an altar tomb of modern date is laid the mutilated figure of a knight in plate armour. Near his head on the wall is* coat with quartering, of eight Nmilies :-1, original coal of the Warburtons (Dutton) 2, fdainwaring, 3, War- burton, 4, Warburton (ancient), 6, Winnington, 6, Grosvenor, 7, Pulford, Phesaunt, with the motto "Je volt droit &wk." Underneath is a marble tablet to
The

a the memor7 of Sir JOhn Warburton who died in 157 Si The North Transept, originally the Dutton chancel, is divided into three cemeteries aparopriated to the families of tne Brookes of Mare, Barry of Marbuty, and Leycester of Tabley. Oa the north side is the m 301.1 • ment of Sir Poter L.,,ycester who died in 1873, the Cheshire historian. The old monument has been re. moved but the former epitaph has been re-inscribed its gold letters on black marble. Over the monument is the G.mily crest and under it the coat of arms. Many _ . .

'interesting tablets to the mlinory of distinguished Cheshire families and persons are to be found on the walls sf the enurch the whole forming an interesting link with the dim and distant past. The village takes its name from the Saxon Bode—a dwelling and Wurth —by water.

THE HEAVY MOTOR TRIALS. The trials this week of heavy motor waggons and the like have aroused ,very great interest in Lancashire, and indeed all over the country. They commenced on Monday and ended on Friday, differ- ent tezti and routes being chosen each day. On Tuesday the motor vehicles, accompanied by a number of light fas-ruoning cars, passed through Warrington the journey being from Liverpool to Manchester. All along the route the liveliest interost was manifested in the event and at War- rington a large crowd assembled in front of the Town Hall, where there was an excellent oppor- tunity of inspecting the vehicles, as the drivers and officials all had lunch in the town. It is not a hilly road through Widnes and War- rington to Manchester—the severest gradient is one in 24—but the many changes of surface help to make the test a real one. All survived it except the vehicle representing Messrs Simpson and Bibby, of Manchester. She broke down at Speke, about eight miles from Liverpool, and it is surmised that the frame was strained owing to over-loading. The others came thr ..tigh in excellent style. There was only one other mishap, and that a slight one. At Warrington the heavy Teorneyeroft, with Re load of about seven tons, was brought to rest over a drain in the stable yard near the 'own Hall. The drain gave way, and one of the wheels sank, and it was a little time before it could be got out with the assistance of a jack and a sister machine. The patrol-driven waggons of Messrs Milner and Co. came out ot the trial very well. Their load is only one of 14. tons each, but then they have only eight horse-power motors, and they are allowed to run up to eight miles an hour, They were the first to arrive in Manchester, going splendidly throughout. One consumed 3i gallons of petrol and the other 4-1 gallons during the journey. The Lancashire Steam Motor Company's vehicle, the Leyland, was next. Tle heavier-laden vehicles -drew up opposite Manchester Town Ball at odd intervals later, and all reported themselves before 8 p.m. After delivering their geode the lurries were driven to Belle Vue, and there they were housed for the night. On Wednesday morning they returned via Bolton and St. Helens, to Liverpool. On Thursday there was a run to Blackburn, and on Friday the return journey to Liverpool. With this the trials were completed. The rep ort of the judges will be issued in October. An "Examiner" representative had the pleasure and privilege of a journey to Manchester from War- rington in the light passenger car reserved for the local committee of the Liverpool Self-Propelled Traffic Association. Councllor A Bennett, the local hon. sec.,was in charge and our full complement,in• eluding the driver,was ten. Starting from the Town Hall, Warrington, at 230 we had a splendid run to Cottonopolis, Deansgate being reached in an hour and a half. During the greater part of the journey the car was travelling a the rate of from fourteen to fifteen miles an hour—in fact a measured mile was covered in four minutes—and this may be con- sidered very fair "going." There were no casual- ties or unforseen stoppages—not even for a punc- ture—which may be due to the fact that our tyres were of solid rubber. The number of people along the route, both in town and village, was amazing and as one of our company remarked the journey was more like the triumphal entry into Pretoria, than a motor-I/Weal trial. The schools starting with Padgate Industrial School and right along as far as Eccles, were all closed during the time the cars were passing,and the children in charge of their teachers were marshalled along the road. Right lustily they cheered, and the object lesson they got in the utility of the horseless carriage would pro. ably not be forgotten very soon. Horses which were passed en route generally showed marked signs of disapproval on the approach of their formid- able rivals, but there was no open revolt. On the other hand it was just as noticeable how supremely unconcerned the cows looked which were occasion- ally overtaken. Of course,their business in life is to provide milk and not to draw goods or passengers, so the advent of the motor does not in the least dis- turb the bovine intellects. It was wonderful to see the ease with which the car we travelled by was manipulated, particularly in the crowded streets of Manchester, where the " tooter " was readily and promptly given precedence. Even a tram stopped its majestic career down Oxford-road in mder that we mignt work our way out of a tight corner. The police were in strong force everywhere but they only winked the other eye when we shot by at a speed which the most kindly-displsed person could not say was within that prescribed by the bye-laws. The dust was the one drawbaek, and that only be- came unpleasant when some speedier car swept by on broad pneumatic tyre. Had the rain of the same evening come but 24 hours earlier our enjoy- ment of the spin would have been entirely tine marred.
