A Witiringiiin Man Hangs Himself. The circumstances attending the shocking suicide of John Spilbury, a wire-drawer, who resided at 150, Ellesmere-street, were inquired into by Mr S Brighouse, County Coroner, at the Police Station on Wednesday. Dora Spilbury, wife of deceased, said he was 39 years of age. Aboat 10 30 on Monday night she and her husband and the four children went to bed.lier hus- band was nnder the inßuence of drink at the time. Shortly after going to bed he became very excited, and said he was going to kill them. She was afraid, and went downstairs with three of the children. Finding all the doors locked, they got out :through the window, andfslept at a neighbour's house. She left the youngest child in the house as she could not get him out. About half-past seven next morn- ing she went home and found all the doors fastened She obtained an entrance to the house by means of the window, and went into the back kitchen,where she found her husband hanging by a silk hanker- chief from the towel roller on the bick door. She procured assistance, and devased was cut down, but life was found to be extinct. For some years deceased had suff3red from severe pains in the head, and had many times threatened to take his life. A verdict of " Suicide, whilst ot unsound mind," was returned. Fearnhead. was summoned at the instance of the Inland Revenue Commissioners, for keeping a carriage without a licence on April 3rd.—Mr Steel represented the defendant. and pleaded guilty to a technical off ence.—The Bench decided to fine the defendant in the cost of the licence (15s) and the tourt costs (21 58 6d in all). ALTIEGED CRUELTY To A KoRBE.—CLERGYMAN CI:YES EVIDENCF.—CA.sE DlsatlssED. —John Corella, • 17, Fennel- street. was summoned for working a pony whilst in an unfit state on the 9th inst.—lnspector Print. R.S.P.C.A.. stated that he was on duty in Church-street, and saw the defendant driving a cream coloured pony attached to a trap, conveying himself, wife, and two children. The animal was proceeding at a trot. Noticing that it was lame he stopped it and on examination found it to be an aged pony in medium condition. It was very lame on the near hind foot. and .'was suffering from spavin. The hock was considerably heated and the animal appeared to be in Pain.—The Rev A S Cameron said he was proceeding along Church-steeet on the date named and saw the pony. He knew it well by, .sight and had often thought it was in a bad condition. On the date in question it was proceeding witn great difEcnll9 and In his opinion it, was exceeoingly cruel to make it draw I such a load.—P.C. Hurst also gave evidence —For the ; defence Mr Perguson, veterinary surgeon, who examined the horse at the request of the defendant, gave evidence. He said he told the defendant that the horse was not fit to be need for the purpose of drawing the trap. In his opinion. I however, the animal had nOt suffered any pain. Witness blistered it in order to reduce the spavin.—lhe magistrates dismissed the Case THE MAINTENANCE or H B IPURNEsS.--Josiah 'Furness, Great Sankey, was summoned to show cause why an order should not be made upon him to contribute to the mainte- nance of his son, Harry Bolton Furness, who is chargeable to the Warrington Union. A DOUBTFUL CASE —William Mottram. of Percival-lane. Runcotn, weer—summoned for trespassing in pursuit of game, on land in the occupation of Mr Ernest Okell, Picco Farm, Runcorn. on the 12th May.—Mr Preston. solicitor. Runcorn. prosecuted—Thomas Jones, a labourer in Mr Okell's employ, testified to seeing Mottram, who was accompanied by a brown lumber dog work the hedges of Six fields as if for game. Later he ordered the defendant off the land, and as he would not go said he would hear more of it. To that defendant replied with oaths, and said if he was summoned be would run a knife into him.— Defendant stated he had permission from Mr Roberts, the , previous tenant of the farm, to go " ratting" on the land. , Mr Roberts was dead ; but he thought that Mrs Roberts was the tenant,and that his permission still held good. He Old not pursue any game, and did not know that the farm was tenanted by Mr Okell.—The case was dismissed. N 3 BIGGVI SCAMP Ile litifiLAND."—John Killgrals, Jabot:ll.er, Weston. and Joseph tAilman, labourer. Pro 1- .ham, were summoned for being drunk and disorderly in Penketh-lane, on the 25th of May.—&liman pleaded not guilty, but Hillgrass did not appear, and a wart ant was issued for his apprehension.—Sergeant Brewster described bow the defendant, along with four or five other,men, created a terrible disturbance in Penketh-lane, and on the fair ground, on the date stated. They had held a boxing show up, and the owner of it was compelled to close It , until the pollee came. Accompanied by Sergeant Gregory he had gone to the spot and succeeded in apprehending two • - of the men but %ingrain and Allman had run off only leaving their caps (produced) behind.—Defendant This is my cap. I don't wear that kind. (Laughter), Superintendent Pear- son , The cap in your hand is a new one though. (Increased laughter).— Continuing Sergeant Brewster de- scribed how the men had savagely assaulted an old man named Creswell, who was 70 years of age, by knocking him down. Waiting for him to rise. and knocking him down again. He had known the defendant about 14 years, and there was no bigger scamp in England "—Sergeant Gregory carrot orated the fact that Allman was present-- Defendant said he was not there, but had no one to prove it. —Defendant who had 17 previous convictions against him, and a bad record at that, was fined £1 Os 64 or 14 days.— ittendant I will have the 14 days. THE only everasting people on earth are the shoemakers. Womrg find horseback riding a sort of one- sided pleasure. POPE says "the proper study of mankind Is man." That may be, but the popular study of man is woman. "LOVERS' QUARRELS," said the philosopher, "are the sham battles that are useful as training for the matrimonial field." MRS. FERRY—" Are your new neighbours well. ?" Mrs. Terry—" I think they are; the children have such awful manners." A RECENT critique upon " Othello " had the following :—" The Moor, seizing a bolster full of rage and jealousy, smothers her. HARRY-" May I kiss you when I get ready to go?" Mabel—" Oh, I'm afraid I shall be so old by that time that you won't care to." "Pi, what is the lull before the storm?" asked Tommy, hopefully. "The honeymoon, my boy," replied the stern parent." MISTRESS: Didn't the ladies who called leave cards?" Bridget: "They wanted to, rpa'am, but I told them you had plenty of your own, and better. too." PARADOXES OF LlFE.—She—" Woman is the weaker vessel, as well you know." He—" Then why is it that man is the oftener broke?" IF some men could come out of their graves and

read the inscriptions on their tombst-ones they would think they had got into the wrong graves. THE Rev. Henry Ward Beecher, describing his new organ, says:—" The swell died in delicious suffocation, like one singing under the bedclothes." I NEVER be at your place of business when a per- son wants to borrow money of you, because if you , are in you will be out, but if you are out you will be in. CHILD, aged six, on seeing a fine engraving of the Assumption: "Mamma, I think little angels' parents must be very poor, for I notice they never have any clothes on. "EVERY man gets the wife that Heaven intended for him," said the young wife. "If that's true," replied her husband, "it strengthens the theory that men are punished for their sins here on earth t" A GENUINE POSER.—" Ma, waz you a bride when you had this photograph taken?" "Yes, Johnny." "Well, ma, if you wuz as pretty as that, what made you go an' marry pa ? " i ON THE WAY HOME. —Jimmy : "Didn't you hear the Sunday-school teacher say your conscience is , 'what tells you when you do wrong?" Tommy: "S It's a good thing it don't tell your mother." SOMETHING OUGHT TO BE DONE.—" My dog is ' almost as intelligent as I am," remarked Squildig. "Are you going to have him shot, or will you try to give him away ?" asked M'Swilligen. A PRACTICAL IDEA.—Blaek : "Suppose we cele- brate our silver wedding next week?" Mrs. Black: "But we have been married.only twelve years." "I know that, but we need the silver." BROWN: "I thought you were a vegetarian, but I hear you eat mutton.' Robinson: "I am not a bigoted vegetarian. I only eat the meat of animals that live on, vegetable food." "I SHOULD like to see somebody abduct me," , said Mrs. Smith at the breakfast table the other morning. " H'm 1 so should I, my dear—so should I," said Mr. Smith, with exceeding earnest- ness. TOM: "Do you believe that marriage, as a rule, is a failure?" Jack: "Judging from my own experience, I believe it is." Tom : "Why, I didn't know that you had ever been married." Jack: "That's just it—l failed to marry." THE LIMIT OF VANITY. Mamma: "I don't t'nk much of dot young man vot's callin' on Re- pecca." Papa: "He's too much shtuck on him- selluf. Vy, dot young fool vould as soon be paid a gompliment as a bill I" WORKS BOTH WAYS.—" The first step towards wealth," says an author, "is the choice of a wife." "And the first step to secnring a good wife is the possession of great wealth," says another. Here we have one of those good rules which work pret- tily both ways. JUDGE: "You have sworn falsely, for the chemists testify that you have poured water into the milk." Milk Peddler: "I have not sworn falsely, your honour. I didn't pour water into the milk, but milk into the water." ENCOURAGING.—"I felt SO sorry, dear, that I I was not at home when you last called on me. ' You won't make me suffer for it, will you dear? but will come again soon even if lam away. Yiur calls always give me such pleasure." His INTENTIONS WERE GOOD.—" Why, Fred- die," exclaimed the mother of a precocious five-year old," aren't you ashamed to call auntie stupid? Go to her at ence and tell her you are very sorry." " Auntie," said the little fellow a few moments later, "I'm awfully sorry you are stupid." THE COMPENSATIONS OF LlFE.—Every mother thinks her babe is the prettiest, every crow believes its young is the whitest, and every bicyclist is assured that his wheel is the best in the market. On the whole, there .is more satisfaction in this world than some persons are willing to admit. Nor SAFE.—Some time ago, in the Court of a certain Scottish burgh, a man was charged with the theft of a pig. The worthy Bailie, in sentenc- ing the prisoner, remarked that pig-stealing in the burgh had lately been too rife, and finished his peroration thus :—" And unless I make an example of you, it's very certain that none of us will be safe." Clams : "I have been in your employ now going on five years, and I am getting the same salary I started with." Proprietor: "I know it, but every time that I've made up my mind to cut you down or discharge you something has reminded me of your wife and little ones at home, and so I just couldn't do it. There, my man, you see I have a heart as well as a head." On Bank Holiday the pretty maiden was poking her lily fingers amongst the seaweed, when a dis- turbed crab fixed her hand. "Oh, Claude 1" she scr9amed to her admirer, who, by-the-by, was a comic writer. "Yes, you are clawed !" he replied, rushing to the rescue; but that wretched pun made her so "crabby" that, as soon as he had released her from her assailant, she gave him his dismissal there and then. "AND so your husband is going away for three months! Dear me 1 How can you ever stand it to be parted from him so long? Why, my hus- band has never been away from me even for a day since we have been married. Whenever he has to go out of town he always takes me with him." "Indeed! that's very nice of him. How long have you been married?" "Nearly three months," the happy young woman @aid, with a delicious sigh. ONE day a professor lost all patience with one of his students, and in a rage told him that he had not the sense of a brute. Upon hearing this the student told him he must apologise. The next morning the professor stood up and said :—" I am called upon to apologise to Mr. for telling him that he has not the sense of a brute, but I now revoke that and say that he has the sense of a brute. A SAD-LOOKING man went into a drug store. "Can you give me," he asked, "something that will drive from my mind the thoughts of sorrow and bitter recollections ? " The druggist nodded, and put up a little dose of quinine, and worm- wood, and rhubarb, and Epsom salts, and a dash of castor-oil, and gave it to him; aud for six months the man couldn't think of anything in the world except new schemes for getting the taste out of his mouth. How HE DISTINGUISHED THEM. —" Johnny, go to the henhouse and see if there are any eggs. Don't bring the china ones, leave them, but if there are any others bring them." Johnny soon returned with half-a-dozen brokon eggs, and his pinafore soiled. His mother seeing him, said "Johnny, how did you break the eggs?" Johnny looked at her in surprise, and said:—" How could I tell if they were china eggs or not until I had tried them?" Jr happened at a restaurant. There was only one vacant seat, and when the quiet, mild-looking clergyman entered he was compelled to take this, opposite a fierce individuai, with fiery whiskers and round spectacles. "I hope Ido not intrude," said the clergyman, meekly. Not at all," replied the other, savagely; "but perhaps you would nob osiiftNtethhveeerre izrafntyineodrnu:akyieol who I am. lam the editor 1 the AnaAna rr cehvies re e nDd y n a gentleman,mitard . ' soothingly; "I have been chaplain to a gaol for twenty years.

div.head: HOSPITAL _ACOOMMODA-
div.p: HOSPITAL _ACOOMMODA-
TION.
Local Government Board Inquiry at Warrington. --- A Long Sitting.

Strong Opposition to the Small Pox Hospital. The Mayor and Corporation Contracts. As a rule Local Government Board inquiries are extremely formal and uninteresting events, but the inquiry whichpwas conducted at the Warrington Town Hall on Saturday proved quite an exception. An application by the Corporation for permission to borrow £9,979 for the provision of a smallpox hospital for Great Sankey, and £BlO2 for the ex- tension of the Borough Infectious Diseases Hospital in Aiken-street, formed the subject of an inquiry which was conducted by Mr E Petronell Manby, M There was a great deal of opposition to the application, and as a consequence the inquiry was protracted to nearly seven hours' duration. Eleven o'clock was the time at which the proceedings commenced and it was not until twenty minutes to six that the inquiry was brought to a close. The proceedings took place in the Council Cham- ber, the Inspector occupying the Mayoral chair. Immediately below him were seated the Mayor and prominent members of the Corporation, and the witnesses to be called in support of the application, whilst the opposition grouped themselves at the other end of the table. Very few members of the general public attended. Principal amongst those present were :—The Mayor (Alderman Roberts), Aldermen Heaton, Shaw-Green and Hutchinson; Councillors Smethurst, William Roberts, Baird, John Roberts. Tinnion, Bennett and Plumpton ; the Town Clerk (Mr J Lyon Whittle), the Deputy-Town Clerk (Mr S Wilson), the Borough Treasurer (Mr J Fairhurst), the Borough Surveyor (Mr T Longdin), Dr Sergeant (medical officer of health for Lanca- shire), Ur Garstang (Altrineliam). Dr Guest Gornall (deputy-medical officer of health ,for rWarrington) ; Mr Samuel Sutton and Me FradleKk.ifoat (repre- senting the Warrington Rural District Council) ; Messrs J Fulton Smith, Thomas Halton, George Thompson, James S Snoddy, James H Smethurst, C Jackson Holmes and Joseph "Smith (appointed at a meeting of Great Sankey ratepayers to form the Hospital Committee and to attend the inquiry), Mr EL Fleming(W B Bishop and Company,Limited) Mr S Gough. Mr James Cliffe, Mr John Pemberton, and Mr Charles Longshaw. The smallvox hospital scheme was first dealt with and the evidence of the Mayor vividly recalled to mind the serious epidemic of 1892-93 and seemed to place beyond doubt the fact that a hospital is required. Stren• uous opposition came from the residents of Great Sankey, the members of the specially appointed committee expressing their opinion on what they regarded as an unsuitable site. Two members of that august body the Ratepayers' and Property Owners' Association (Messrs S Gough and J Clare), and Mr J Pemberton, who has recently distinguish- ed himself in the matter of alleged " Corporation scandals," opposed the scheme on economical grounds, urging that the present financial position of the Borough dRI not warrant the expenditure, Several heated arguments between • these gentle- men and the Mayor took place, questions entirely out of the scope of the inquiry continually cropping up. The Inspector allowed the opposition plenty of latitude in fact, he seemed a little to generous at times. Frequent passages at arms arose with reference to contracts, &c., but the opponents to the application were not allowed to go too deeply into these matters. It was about five o'clock when the inquiry into the first portion of the application terminated, so that not much time was occupied in dealing with the pro- posed extension of the Fever Hospital. Mr Gough wanted the inquiry adjourning so that the matter could be more fully gone into but the Inspector refused to agree to:this. Evidence was then given in support ot the second part of the application,ancl this gave Messrs Gough and Company another 1 opportunity of displaying their abilities in cross- examination. The inspector announced that he would visit the proposed site of the small pox hospital on the following Tuesday. NOTICE OF THE INQUIRY. A HOST OF OBJECTIONS. Directly the Town Clerk had read the notice of the inquiry, Me Gorron said he shou'd like to ask whether he was entitled to see the application for the order. He made application to the Town Clerk but was refused per- ml sinn. He was told there was only a communication. Be thought the ratepayers ought have been in posirssion of the details of the order so that they could make objection to it. The INSPECTOR : lam here to hear objections. Mr FLEMING : We have heard nothing about this large sum of money, and I have been requested by a large firm in the town to lodge an objection to the expenditure. I should like to say a good deal on the matter when I sin in order. Mr CLIFFE : The ratepay era are quite entitled to have information given to them in the public press. I venture to suggest that ninety-nine ratepayers out of every hundred know nothing about the inquiry. The Council are attempting to keep the ratepayers in the dark. The Irispecroa asked the Tow a.Clerk to produce evi- dence that the notices had been posted in the usual way. The Towx CLERK explained that a gentleman applied for a copy of the order and his clerk told him that the application had been made in the Usual way. The resolution of the Town Council with regard to the new hospital was passed unanimously on the 30th October, 1900, ard the proceedings of the Council were duly re- ported in all the local newspapers. The INSPECTOR: There is no doubt the notizes have been posted throughout the district ? The Tows CLERK: No doubt. The INSPECTOR (to the objectors): You maintain that you have not received sufficient notice? Mr PEMBERTON said he raised the same objection. He was a member of the firm of "Mainwating and Pem- berton." He had received no notice of the inquiry,nor bad he seen any notices anywhere about the town. Mr Charles LoNostosweaid he supported the gentle- men who had just spoken. The ISPPECTOR remarked that the notices appeared to have been posted to the usual places, and he had a list of a large number of places in his possession. There was no adverthrement. The TOWN Ca- ex: No, sir. The INSPECTOR: It is not usual to advertise. Mr Gomm: I have seen only about three posters, and that is not much to convince 60,000 inhabitants. The INSPECTOR: The fact that you have seen one notice la good enough for the purpose of toe inquiry. kdr CLIFFE: I never saw the notice until Wednesday last, Mr Goron asked whether the Municipal Corporation Acts or the Public Health Act made provision that the ratepayers should be supplied with the details of the application ? The INSPECTOR: Not individually. How would you send to every individual ratepayer? Mr Gopon : If a ratepayer makes an application provision ought to be made for that application to be attended to. The TowN CLERK : There is nothing to show these gentlemen except a copy of the order and the resolution of the Council. Mr GEORGE THOMPSON said he attended to represent a committee of the ratepayers of Great Sankey. At thelproper time he should like to be heard. He merely objected to the site of the building for the hospital. Mr GOUGE(: It is our intention to make a written application to the Board of Trade. The INSPECTOR: The Board of Trade have nothing to do with the matter. (Laughter.) It is the Local Government Board. Mr GOUGH : Ibe your pardon. The INSPECTOR: You propose to make a formal Com- plaint to the Local Government Board. Mr GOUGH : Yes, to the borrowing of the money. The INSPECTOR: And the Board will be pleased to receive your application and consider it with my report. Albert BARE, a bill-poster was called and proved that 90 notices had been posted in the borough and 15 or 16 in Great Sankey. The notices were posted a week ago the previous day. Mr Gooon : They are small bills ; not much to call the attention of the public to an inquiry. The INSPECTOR : It is the official notice issued by the Local Government Board. The Town Council of War- ringten have nothing to do with them. The TOWN CLERK: The notices have been nrinted in London. The matter then dropped. , THE FIRST BREEZE. MR. HALTON UNDER A MISAPPRENENSION. THE PEAR TREE FARM SITE. The TOWN CLERK in opening the case for the Cor- poration explained that Mr J H Gornall, the medical officer for Warrington, was unable to be present owing to indisposition. THE MAYOR'S EVIDENCE. QUESTIONS BY MESSRS. PEMBERTON AND GOUGH. HEATED REMARKS. The MAYOR as deputy chairman of the Health Corn - mittee, then gave evidence in the absence of the chair- man (Alderman Sutton). His Worship said that in the. year 1892-3 they had a very serious epidemic of small- pox which carried away nosily valushle lives and laid large numbers of families under serious financial obli- gations. The east to the borough was over £lO,OOO. He bad to apologise for the absence of the chairman (All the committee, Who was not well and a ho was taking much-needed rest. Continuing he said tbB outbreak was the most serious that had. occurred in his (the speaker's) lifetime, and they were absolutely unprepared to deal with itaf speaking as ia7man he had no hesitation in saying, 'that the epidemic assumed its very serious proportions In a great measure owing to the fact of their unprell paredness. There was no hospital other than the ordiL nary infectious diseases hospital which had been occu- pied by the ordinary fever cases. The committee had to sit from day to day and to make such accommeda- , tion as was possible under the extraordinary circum- stances. They took an old works in the town and adapted it as well as they could, and from that day the Icommittee had felt the responsibility which rested upon them not to lose more time than was necessary in pro- viding adsquate means to cope with any outbreak that might arise, large or small. They had been advised that It was not consistent to treat smallpox cases at an or- dinary infectious diseases hospital, and acting under that advice they had submitted plans for a new hospi- tal. The committee load spent a considerable amount of time in visiting various suggested sites. Mr CLIFFE : They got well paid for it. The Tow)? CLERK: I object to that remark. The INSPECTOR : It 15 not fair to make such a state- ant in public. Mr CLIFFE (to the Mayor) : Are you not interested in this matter ? The MAYOR: Yes, lam interested as the deputy- chairman of the Health Committee, and as a man whose action is open to the observation of anybody in Warrington. Mr CLIFFE Have you sold the Slate Company to your wite or!son ? The Mayes : I have not sold the Slate Company to anybody. The Tovfx CLERK objected to the introduction of such personal matters, and the Inspector said they were out of order, Tioe MAYOR explained why the Pear Tree Farm site was unsuitable. A very serious difficulty was its proxi- mity to Poulton-witta-Fearnhead, which was becoming,in fact had became a comparatively populous district. In 1899 a site was suggested at Great Sankey by Councillor Smethurst, who was a member of the Committee, and simultaneously the present site was suggested. It was dose to the site suggested by Councillor Smethurst. The Committee visited both the sites, either of which was much preferable to the Pear Tree Farm site, but in the judgment of the Committee the present site was con- sidered tbe better of the two. He did not think the price to be paid was extravagant, but it was fully as much as it was worth. Mr Gouoa : Have you bad experience of the value of land ? ' The MAYOR: A little. In answer to Mr Pemberton HIS Woßsfue said the epidemic cost over £IO,OOO. The total cost to the town was £10,400. Mr PESIBERTON : From the report of the Medical Officer of Health on tho epidemic, a copy of which I have before me, it appears that included in the cost of the small-pox epidemic is the charge for a largo number of scarlatina cases and other expenses which would have been incurred even if there had not been an epidemic. The cost for Hope Hospital was £4,477 ts 4d. The MAYOR : If you cannot understand the almost insurmountable difficulty which follows the conversion of an ironworks long disused into the purpose of a hospital anything I can say won't convince you. . Mr PEMEEBToN : That is not a fair way to put the. matter. The MAYOR: It is the way I put it. I knew Warring- ton:before you came to it. THE BOROUGH SURVEYOR EXPLAINS. FULL DETAILS OF THE SCHEME. • ' 1 Mr THOMAS LONGDIN, the Borough Surveyor: then made an exhaustive statement as to • the in Untions of the Corporation. He said he had beef& Borough Surveyor for 23 years and in connection whirl the Health Committee had beers trying to get a site, for the hospital for dart years. Owing to the require- ments of the L )eal Government Board they had ex-1 , perienced grest difficulty in finding a suitable site. Irl' 1E99 they were forced as a committee to suggest the Pear Tree Farm site to the C •uneil. A memorandum With reference to the construction of hospitals was lesued by, the Local Government Board in 1900: The Pear Treel Farm site could never have been adopted to suit these, requirements. apart from that.plans were submitted t the Board; and so many alterations !ore requires owing to the position of the site, that the cost would( have been about £12,C00. The ground about was a strong clay which would have necessitated overcoming the difficulties of drainage. There was a population of 800 within a half mile radius. It was a physical impossibility to find a suitable site in the borough, and 20 visits had been ;Aid to various places, Visits were also made outside the borough. The present site fulfilled all the rs quieements of the Local Government Beard. ' The site on the ordnance map was known as " Smart's Hpuse." The land was Ili acres in extent, It was a healthy site and was bounded by fields and a brook and an occupation road that led to a farm. The Corpora- tion at present only proposed to utilize 3i acres of land, leaving the cemaining portion for future extension. The land would have a close fence 61 feet high. The site was a little under four miles from the centre of the town. Within a quarter of a mile of the zone there were three houses with a population of 17 ; within half a mile 28 houses and a population of 148, and within the three- quarter mile radius 56 houses and 398 population. They proposed to construct septic tanks and bacteria beds. The land and buildings would cost £8.619,the iron work in connection with the sewage tanks £2OO, the furnish- ing £250, the water supply £450, disinfector £ll3O ; special ambulance £l2O, clerk of the works and assist- ants £l6O, total £9,979. THE OBJECTIONS FROM GREAT SANKEY. FORMAL PROTEST. A formal protest against the site was presented by the Great Sankey Committee and was read by Mr Thompson. The first part of the protest se!: out the fact that a parish meeting had been held respecting the proposed small-pox hospital at which the owners of pro. perty, residents, and ratepayers had discussed the question, and ultimately a committee had been appointed to represent the parish on the question. The protest proceeded—" And whereas at the last meeting of the said committee held on Tuesday the 28th ult, the said notice of inquiry was read, and after a lengthy dis- cussion it was resolved :—' Thit a formal written pro- test be handed in at tie inquiry and that the same be supported by the attendance of as many members of the committee as can make it convenient :to be present.'" It was also decided to add by way of further explaining the objection already stated that the proposed site is unsuieable by reason of the ground being fiat, having a clay subsoil, and that excavations for a foundation would prove that water layl within a few feet of thesur- face, also that the conveyance of patients would be along the main road from Manchester to Liverpool which runs through the centre of the town, and that no less than six public schools would have to be passed en that section of the road reckoning from the Town Hall as the starting point to the Great Sankey Board schools, the last named school alone containing over 300 schol- ars, and further that the most densely populated part of thelborough is on the opposite or easterly side of the borough, and thus the greater number of cases would be brought through or across the centre of the town. It was further contended that the site should not be on the westerly side of the borough, inasmuch as the pre- vailing winds 'would carry any infection from the hos- pital towards the town. The committee, moreover, respectfully suggested that the seven days- notice of ' the inquiry (covering the Whitsuntide holidays) might reasonablybe put forward as too store a space to allow , for obtainpg evidence of a stronger character against the suitability of the site proposed, which would have been done had time permitted. Mr FULTON SMITH said that naturally the people had a dread of small-pox, and the committee were only doing their duty in making that protest on behalf of the rate- payers. The SURVEYOR: We found it absolutaly impossible, to utilize Pear Tree Farm for a hospital. It would cost considerably more than at Sankey. THE TREATMENT OF EFFLUENT. Dr GARSTANG then gave evidence in favour of the Great Sankey scheme. He had, he said, been medical officer for six years to five districts—one rural and four urban—in Cheshire and Staffordshire. He had visited the site at Great Sankey and carefully inspected it, and it was an exceptionally good one. As the Medical Officer of the Bucklow Joint Board, he had been hunting for small-pox sites for three years, and the prices had ranged for the land from £3OO to £7OO an acre. His Board had not paid that sum, and they were still look. ing for a site they could cake without compulsory powers. Taking into consideration the thickly popu- lated district, of which Warrington was the centre, it appeared to him to be extremely unlikely that at any point round Warrington, and within the same distance, another site could be found which would contain a similar population within the prohibited area. The sewerage works wore sufficient for a very much larger

place. Any small-pox poison which might be conveied into the tanks would be absolutely destroyed during the time the sewage remained under treatment. He bad not the slightest objection to give it as his opinion, and pledge his reputation, that the effluent ultimately enter- ing the brook would be very little different to ordinary clear, pure, land water.—By Mr Toompson.—Efe had visited the site once. In answer to Mr Halton, he Town CLERK said the Corporation would not undertake to pipe the brook the whole, length. Witness said it would be absolutely safe for any number of cittle to drink from the brook. MORE MEDICAL EVIDENCE. DOES INFECTION CARRY IN THE AIR ? Dr SARGEANT Medical Office of Elealth to the Lanca- shire County Council said he had been engaged in sanitary work for over a quarter of a century entirely. He had a great deal of knowledge with respect to hospital schemes, and for dealing with small-pox. He had no doubt there was a necessity for a small-pox hospital, and the site selected was eminently suitable. Dr GUEST GORNALL said it was a matter cf regret that his father, who was really responsible for recom- mending the site to the Corporation trom the Public Health standpoint, was not able to be present, but it was not inappropriate that he (Dr Guest Gornall) should have something to say about the matter seeing that he was intimately mixed up with the events which had brought the necessity for a small-pox hospital in the town to the notice of the Corporation. A hospital should be situated in a neighbourhood where is was not in close contact with a thickly populated area. Be had examined the site in question at Sankey on two once-

•sions, and he had come to the conclusion that it was an admirable one, open, healthy and eminently suited to the treatment of patients, and possessed such natural features as to render, drainage easy and successful. It possessed what to his mind was a mast important qualification. It was situated in a sparsely populatea neighbourhood and would reduce to a minimum the chance of the hospital, even if full of patients, being in any sense a danger to the neighbour- hood which was not the case in the year 1892-3 when they had a crowded hospital in the middle of Warring- ton. The arrangements which had been Mentioned would be sufficient to render the effluent not only com- paratively pure but also free from any danger of spreading the disease. Mr THOMPSON expressed his regret at the absence of the Medical Officer, and hoped he would soon be amongst them again. In answer to Mr Thompson. Dr Guest Gornall said that the processes of putrefaction were known to kill the germs of disease. That was a Matter that had been worked out carefully by expert scientists. In answer to Mr Snoddy the Comm said the ventila- tion would be carried out by the ordinary means. The INSPECTOR : Your suggestion is that there should be some arrangements for cremating the foul air ? Mr SHODDY: Yes. sir. The INSPECTOR : And the doctor does not think It necessary. Alderman HEATON : How far is the poisoned air supposed to travel ? Dr GOnNaLL : It is simply a matter of theory that it carries at all through the air. It is. perhaps, a theory which is needed to explain certain facts, but it cannot be regarded as proved. By Mr PEMIERTON : He did everything in connection with the Hope Smallpox Hospital. He issued the re- port now produced. The question w 53 still unanswered, as far as he knew, how far infection travelled. Mr TIrOMPSON said that he and the gentlemen with him were not satisfied with the reports made by the medical gentlemen present,apd they would throw them- selVes on the Local GOvernMettt Board to see that they were protected from anything that might happen from the pollution, of the brook and from infection of any kind. Mr Suopnt : And provision has not been made for disinfecting the air. That we would especially point out. THE FINANCIAL POSITION OF THE BOROUGH. THE OVERDRAFT AT 'THE BANK. The second portion of the inquirylwas then proceeded with. The Tows CLERK said this matter of the extension had been pressed upon the Corporation by the Local Government Board. Mr Goma : You think conveying patients would be dangerous to the neighbourhood and possibly lead to contagion. Councillor PLUMPTON : It would cause property to depreciate in value. The Towsr CLERK: Self-interest again. (Laughter.) The InsrEcron : As far as I know there is no evid- ; ence whatever of the communication of infection through the air except in the case of small-pox ; it If not necessarily certain, I believe. Some opinions are that it is thus conveyed ; others that it is not. Mr PEMBERTON said this was an inopportune moment to spend more, when they were providing out district& The MAYOR: When the Borough requirements make it impossible to take out-patients they are not taken. , Mr PEMBERTON : My point is that we should not fino the capital sum for other people. Mr Govan : We ought to have waited, considering our indebtedness. We are administering in this towo with closed doors. Dr GUEST GORNALL gave evidence, and said the plane were eminently suitable. An administrative block vise wanted. The day and night nurses bad to occupy the beds in turn—a condition of things which would not he allowed in a lodging-house. Two of the laundry ino,il slept in an old hut (wooden), and the laundresses :01r Lived outside ths balding for years, The old would be used for isolation eases, doubtful caseS all convalescent cases. Mr GOMM : Is your father an interested party in trg Slate Company ? (Laughter.) The INSPECTOR : His father is not here, and I &fit think you can expect him to answer that question. Mr Gouoil : Is it not an extravagant amount? I col? ,eider this is nothing more or less than snatching a case without giving us a fair chance of being represented te defend the case. The INSPECTOR: The Town Council have nothing r 0 . do with fixing the date of the inquiry. The MAYOR : Everything connected with the apPlt, cation has been fully discussed in public in the Coupe,' Chamber, and fully reported ia the local press frolO to time. Mr PEMBERTON : I did not know about the inquirs; until nine o'clock on Thursday night. I think it ougb to be advertized in the local:press. • The Insnaron made a note of the statement. This concluded the inquiry.

A DOUBLE THRASHING. Boy Runs away from Padgate Industrial ProceedingsneieiotScth:etool At the co ordinary k en business at the Warrinoton Police Court on Friday morning, Mr A Browne, on heti-al-of the N S.P.C.C. made a somewhat singular appLcation. He said that that morning a little boy named Joseph William Bowen came to the Police Station (which he (Mr Browne) submitted was a place of Safety within the meaning of the Act under which the application was made) for protection. Haying ascertained what was the matter with him the police called in lespectGr Hackett who took the boy to Dr Bowdea to be examined. He (Mr Browne) now asked tOr an order for the boy's custody in a place of safety until further instructions were received from the society's head office. r C Pnillips was called and stated that the boy came to the Police S:ation that morning, He said he had tun away from Padget, Industrial schools because he had been thrashed. 11-• was sent to Dr Bowden. The by in question, Jo ph William Bowen, aged 13 years, stated that on Thursday afternoon he and four other boys at the radgate Industrial Schools were playioa with a bicycle belonging to a Mr McKibbin. pee of the tyres cot punctured, and he and another boy were ' blamed for it and thrashed • HP was stripped, and Mr Wright, the Superintendent, gave him five strokes with A cane and sent him to bed. Afterwards he came down for a drink, and Mrs McKibbin thrashed him with a walking stick. At five o'clock !hat mornino he ran away from the Schools with his tir,Aher and came to the Police Station. The boy's brother said he ran away because be " would always he getting the stick." He was not thrashed on Thursday. Ultimately he expressed his willineness to go back to the schools. Mr Browne said he asked for an order under Section 5, of the Prevention of Cruelty t Children Act, which" provided that if a child in respect of sonom an offence of cruelty within the meaning of the Act had been nem. mitted, sought refuge in a place of safety he might be detained and brought before the Court and the Court ini../ht make an order for him to be kept in a place of safety. Continuing he said that on the advice of Dr Bowden the Society proposed to take certain proceed- ings and they asked for the boy to be committed to, the Workhouse until they issued a summons. The bly was strioped in Court and it was seen that there were a number of weal marks acrcss his back which he alleged had been inflicted by Mr Wright and Mrs McKibbin. Mr Browne said there were other old marks. The Bench made an order for his detention in the Workhouse for 14 days.

div.head: SCHOOL HOLIDAYS AT
div.p: THE SCHOOL HOLIDAYS AT
WARRINGTON.
Alteration ot Date.

--- It has ben customary in Warrington for many years for the elementary day school children to , commence their summer holidays during Walking Day week, but this year an alteration has been decided upon. The children have quite recently returned to school after an enforced holiday of three weeks owing to the epidemic of measles. and it is felt undesirable to have another break of three weeks or a month almost immediately after re-opening the schools, for the usual summer holi- days. Furthermore it has long been felt that the summer holidays of the school children in Warring- ton are held too early in the year. The managers of the Roman Catholic Schools, with the °Dint of meeting the difficulty, decided to commence the holidays a month later,but the othervoluntar y school managers did e t fall in with the arrange- ment, and it only tended to confuse matters. This year, however, there is every probability Of all the schools in the town breaking tip for the summer holidays on July 26th. The tuatiapers of the Church of England schools have fixed upon this dee and there is a probability that all school managers will come to a like con- clusion. At the meeting of the Great Sankey School Board on Tuesday it was decided to hold the school holidays at the same time as at Warrington. A uniform holiday will greatly facilitate the work of the School Attendance offi:ers who have experi- enced great difficulry in former years owing to the different arrangernsnts existing at various schools. The children will is) granted a Ipliday on Walk- ing Day but the schools will re-commence on the following Monday and continue until July 26,when the break-up for the sum-ner holidays will take place.

-tBRINGTON AND MID•OHESHIRE EXAMINER. ,ARLESTOWN AND NEWTON EXAMINER, NCORN EXAMINER. WIDNES EXAMENER. ST. HELENS EXAMINER:
EXAMINER PRINTING OFFICE.
Ettttrs to the ebttor. NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS.
Authors of letters intended for publication must In all cases send their names and addresses to the Editor.
Matters intended for publication must be written on one side only of the paper and sent in. if possible,
not latter than- Thursday: Correspondents are strongly advised to write . . . . . . .
briefly. A short letter has much greater chance of insertion than a long one. We cannot under ordinary circumstances under- take to return the manuscripts which are not used.
Municipal Election Compromises and
Corporation Contracts.

Sir,—Your correspondent "Maxim "evidently knows more about bow the town has been governed than I gave him credit for, but his kaowlege of persons seems to be very vague' Not having entered this controversy under a nom de plitme it is not necessary for me to en- lighten him further as Lo my identity, suffice it to say I am still in the town that gave me b,rth and of which I am exceedingly proud. " Maxim " wishes me to tell him when the town was not politically governed and goes back to the old days of political warfare when gentlemen like Mr John Crosfield, Mr alderman Francomb, Mr Alderman Sutton and the late Messrs Greening and Broadbent all had to fight their way into the Council, and I maintain that when a man has been elected to the Council by the votes of the electorate be esteems it a greater honour and holds his seat with more pride than he would if elected otherwise. Yes, the Government of our town has always been political and so long as we have two recognised parties I cannot see any other way out of it. If lam any judge of the characteristics of my fellow townsmen they like a fair fight. "Maxim" goes on to say that this compact was brought about for the purpose of keeping down expenses and for each party to fill the place as vacancies occur without a contest. " Maxim" forgets people are given to change. Take, for instance, Latchford Ward, which was always looked upon as the Gibraltar of Toryism. In a fair contest the Conserva- tive candidate had not the shadow of a chance with his Liberal opponent, but on the first vacancy occurring he was fostered on the Ward without a contest. The same alsogoccurred with Bewsey Ward. 1 Here we have two instances where the wishes of the people have been com- pletely set atinaught by the introduction of this compact. Is not this a complote violation of the liberty of the people ? " Maxim " infers because this question has been taken up so earnestly that it has been done with the object of casting reflections upon the character of certain gentlemen of the town. Nothing of the kind. It has been done for the purpose of vindicating the rights and liberties of the people. I question whether the gentlemen named are aware of the discontent which is so prevalent in the town upon this question. The lane.' part of " Maxim's " letter is very much uncalled for, It would have been more appropriate had it appeared some three months ago when your pages were occupied with correspondence rs Corporation Contracts. Why has he7remained silent so long ? It is not because of the respect for the gentlemen who were responsible for those letters. It ill becomes a man to talk of the cowardice of others when he writes under an assumed name. Come out Mr Maxim and show yourself worthy of those characteristics which have made the name of Englishmen famous throughout the whole world—of striking;hard but never below the belt. I remain yours t espectf ully,
J. MARSH.
jt

div.head: ARE WOMEN GROWING WISER?
div.p: ARE WOMEN GROWING WISER?
To THE EDITOR OF THE" VI ARRINGTON EXAMINER."

Dear Sir,—Your correspondent " Amelia" flies too high altogether in her estimate of women's wisdom. lo my estimation, a woman's borne, her husband, and her children should be her pride and care. The comfort of the home, and the wants of her husband and little ones should be her study. Not only should she meet their requirements when in health, but also when " out of sorts." To do this successfully requires some know- ledge of homely and effective rneoicines. Yet how little real knowledge many women possess on such subjects may be gauged by the amount of money spent on worthless and inexpensive medicines. Fortunately one is glad to note the rapidly-increasing use of a remedy like Charles Forde's Bile Beans for Biliousness in this connection. The wisdom of house- wives who always keep a box of this wonderful veget able preparation on their shelves is to be commended Attacks of "the blues" brought on by indigestion headache, sleeplessness, or some other " little " ailment are fruitful sources of family unhappiness; and the woman wbo by judicious use of this natural vegetable remedy brings an end to these ailments occurring either in herself, busband,or children,to my mind shows much wisdom. "Amelia" may talk about the " bad temper and boorishness" of modern men as she chooses, but she should not forget that health often governs temper. A little money spent on Bile Beans as a preventative of, or cure for iedigestion—and, incidentally, bad temper— would show more practical wisdom that much philoso- phising.—Youre,
CONSTANT RE IDER.

div.head: TEMPERANCE MISSION AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: TEMPERANCE MISSION AT WARRINGTON.

During the past week, the Rev L M Isitt, of New Zeal‘nd, has conducted a succe'sful temperance mission in Warrington. Notwithstanding the fact that the weather has had a tendency to keep people out of doors the attendance at the meetings has been encouraging and much good work has been done. Mr. Isitt at Wycliffe P.S.A. Meeting.

The first meeting in connection with the Rev Is M Isi t's Temperance Mission was held on Sunday after- noon when he addressed the P.S.A. men at Wyzliffe Church. Members of other P.S.A.'s in the town were in attendanca and there was a large and encourae- ing gathering. The Rev John Yonge presided and in introducing Mr Isitt, said he was glad that gentleman had coma to Warrington. He did not think they had had a big temperance mission in Warrington , since Edward Murphy was here. That was a very successful mission And some permanent good was done. ,He would like to see a repetition of that sort of thing at the present mission. It was sadly needed in War_ ington. Until the churches and the intelligent works ingmen of the town woke up on this question there wa very little hope of Christianity making any progress in Warrington. (Hear, bear). Mr Isitt ,then delivered telling address. He said be was an exceedingly moder ate man, and if in the course of his addresses they ells covered any exaggeration or any untruths they must let him know of them. He hoped they were going Co have a good time in Warrington. He proceeded to demonstrate that alcohol was an irritant poison and was an described in the medical dictionaries. Did they mean to tell him that it could be a good thing to go on taking into the system in a diluted form an irritant poison ? T e speaker then went on to prove that life was shortened by our present drinking habits. It was scientifically wrong to take alcohol into the system and we paid the penalty by a shorter life. This had been demonstrated by the insurance socicties,who had proved that a teetotaler's life was cf longer duration than that of the moderate drinker or drunkard. Mr Isitt made a strong appeal to the moderate drinkers to sign the pledge and give up the taking of intoxicants. The one difficulty in the way cf effective temperance reform was the indifference of the respetotable moderate drinker —At the conclusion of the address, pleclee cards were taken round by a number of ladies and 72 signatures were obtained.

div.head: Opening Service at Parr Hall.
div.p: Opening Service at Parr Hall.

The mission was commenced on Sunday evening, when an address was given by the missioner. There was an exceedingly god attendance, representatives from most denominations being present. the chair was occupied by the Rev F E Powell, vicar of St. James', Latchford, and supporting him on the platform were the Revs L M Isitt, E T Reed (Reformed Episcopal Church), John Yonge (Wycliffe Congregational), Coun- cillors W lt,berts and Ellison, and Messrs Bolland and Farrar. A choir was alao in attendance, conducted by Councillor W Stough, the organ being presided over by Mr T Brough.

_ I The CHAIRMAN thought of late that they had empha- sised the political and social aspects of the temperance question—and they could not emphaize them too much —yet they might be in danger of losing sight of the personal and individual side of the temperance problem, which, after all, was the more important. There were thousands of those around them being hurried into premature graves through the pernicious habit of ex- cessivo drinking. So they must not neglect to warn such of their danger even while they pressed their legislators to come to their assistance. If Mr Isitt could do anything to remove the prevailing apathy which, to his mind, was an evil not muLch less than the intemper- ance it appeared to condone, they would welcome his efforts and would be glad he had come in their midst. It was no argument that it was only the sympathisers with thA movement who attended such meetings as these. For they were the very ones they wished to stimulate to further efforts. The duty of combating the evil was not the work of such as Mr Isitt alone, but of every individual who had the welfare of his kindred at heart.
The Rev L M Isirr addressed the mein e on the subject of' The Chuzch and the Liquor Traffic."

div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.
LATEST TELEGRAMS
Daring British Exploit.
Boers Surprised and Defeated. 37 Killed.
PRETORIA, Wednesday.

Colonel Wilson, commanding the 2nd Kitch- ener's Scouts, hearing that Commandant Beyers had sent an advance commando of over 400 men north in charge of all his supplies pre- paratory to his retirement with his main force, decided to attack the convoy, The attack was carried out with complete success The Boers were completely surprised, but resisted stubbornly for a time. On Kitch- ener's fighting scouts pressing home toe attack they broke and fled, leaving all their supplies on the field and 37 dead. Our lo,s was three killed and 15 wounded. We captured 8,000 cattle and eighteen wag- gons. All the supplies which could not be taken were burned.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
The Tramways and Light Railway Schemes.

The monthly meeting of the Warrisgton Town Council was held at the Town Han on Tuesday evening, the Mayor (Alderman Roberts) presiding. There were also present Aldermen Fairclough (deputy Mayor), Bolton. Francomb, Shaw Green, Heston, flutchinPon Sutton, Councillors Benn,tt, Brough, Burton, Davies. , Duncan. James Evans, JMn Evans, Ellison, Forshaw, Greening, Flulse, A J Jolley, A Jolley, Malkin, Peacock, Plumpton, FR Roberts, J Roberts, W Roberts, Rogers, Sampson, Shillcock, Smethurst, finnion and Wilkinson with Messrs 3 L Whittle (Town Clerk) S Wilson (Deputy Town Clerk), J Fairhurst (borough treasurer), T Longdin (borough surveyor), J Deas (water engineer), and W 8 Haddock (gas engineer). A Question of Procedure.

Before moving ne adoption of the minutes of the ' thatch Committee the Mayor wished to refer to a ques- tion raised at the last meeting of the Council in refer- ence to a certain matter of procedure. He then ex- pressed an opinion which, upon further consideration he had reason to believe was inaccurate. The question was as to whether a member of the Council was entitled to refer to the minutes of a committee, such minutes not being sunmitted for the confirmation of the Council but which happened to be minutes under consideration on the dates of the minutes which were required to be confirmed. He then said that he did not think any member of the Council was entitled to refer ta any minutes except those printed on the agenda paper. Upon further oon- sideration, and after consultation with the Town Clerk, he was of the opinion that the opinion he then expresseo was incorrect and any member would be perfectly in order in referring to any minutes of the committee which happened to be within the dates named by the minutes submitted for confirmation.
Watch Committee—The Lighting of the New Police Buildings.

On May 16th, the Watch Committee considered the tenders for fitting and wiring for electric lighting at the new policf, premises : It was resolved chat the tenders of Mr Henry Ingham and the Warrington and District Electric Light and Power Co„ Limited, be referred to Mr Grimsdale to report thereon, and that the Deputy- Mayor be authorized to accept the tender recommended by him. In moving the confirmation of the minutes the MAYOR said that on the recommendation of Mr Grim- dale,tne Deputy-Mayor had accepted the tender of Mr Ingham, and it would b 3 submitted to the next Council meeting for approval. The minutes were confirmed, Seats and Trees at Bridge Foot.

The Street Improvement and Lign—ting Committee recommended that in laying out the Laud at Bridge Foot provision be made for the planting of trees and that three seats be provided for the use of the public. It was also recommended that two seats be provided and placed under the trees near Black Lion Bridge, Wilders- pool Causeway. The minutes were approved. Councillor Bennett and '' Smoke Nuisances." • Insanitary Property.

- The minutes °lithe Health Committee stated that the Medical Officer of Health having reported the following houses belonging to the Corporation as unfit for human habitation, v z : 375, Golborne-street ; 2, Daliam-lane ; and two EIJUSeS in Twiss's Yard, Wilderspool Causeway. It was resolved that the houses be demolished. At a meeting of the committee on May 15th, it was resolved that Dr John Guest Gornall be appointed a:puty Medical Officer of Health, subject to the ap- proval of the Local Government Board, and the Deputy Medical Superintendent of the Hospital for Infectious' Diseases. The resignation of Dr John Hankinson Gornall as Public Analyst was accepted with regret, and it was resolv( d that Dr John Guest Gornall be appointed Public Analyst at a sAlary of £5O per annum, subject to :he approval of the Local Government Board.
Aldermsn Surrorr moved the adoption of the minutes and the Mayor seconded. . . .

Councillor FORSUAW thought the appointment of public analyst ought to be defernid until the question of the appointment of Medical Officer came forward. Councillor BENNETr expressed regret at the continued indisposition of Dr Gornall and offered a word of con- gratulation on his annual report. It was always extremely interesting and on this occasion was prob- ably more interesting than Usual. Smile points m ra- tioned required atteation, one of them having becoine highly objectionable. The first matter was that or insanitary property. In the report he noticed that a large number of insanitary houses were reported as not having been attended to. He should like to know how it was that houses which were insanitary were allowed to remain in that state. It must be detrimental to public health. Pro- ceeding to refer to the report of Inspector Church with regard to smoke nuisances, Councillor Bennett said he thought be was like" a voice crying in the wilderness " on this subject but he intended to go on cryieg even if he made himself a nuisauce. He should not be satisfied until the committee did its duty with regard to the smoke nuisance which was one of the greatest curses under which they lived at the present time. ft was an intoler- able nuisance going on from slay to day and hour to hour, and the report was simply a farce B icause they cou.d not deal with large iron works, it was no excuse why they should not deal with other works. They did not want to interfere With local enterprises, but they ought to exercise reasonable pressure in order to induce manufacturers to exercise more care. The nuisance did not effect those members who went out into the country and thus got away from the smoke but there were some who in spite of the high rates, lived in town, and they ought to be considered and not suffocated without protest. Councillor 1311L9E, as being connected with a large manufacturing concern, considered the remarks of Councillor Bennett to be totally unjustified. As far as his firm was concerned they had the most expert stokers they could get and they were carefully watched. Councillor TINNION was of opinion that, considering the large and varied manufactures carried on, Warring- ton was remarkably free from a see iske nuisance. He thought that the matter did not concern the Health Committee and ought to have been mentioned when the minutes of the Sanitary Committee came forward. Alderman Bovecier also expressed himself in similar terms. , In replying to Councillor Forshaw, AldermaniSueroe said that it was necessary that the committee should appoint Dr Guest Gornall to be public analyst and not deputy analyst because there were certain duties in connection with the office which could only be performed by the public analyst himself and not by a deputy. With regard to the insanitary property, as tar, as the committee was concerned they had done all they possibly could. They bad viaited prcperty and had given instructions to the officials to take action in the cases where it was necessary Perhaps the reason why it had not been done in all cases waS on acc eunt of the illness of the Medical Officer: With regard to the smoke nuisance bethought it should have been brought forward when the minutes of the Sanitary Works Committee were considered. He was to some extent agreed with Councillor Bennett that it was desirable to abate the nuisance as much as poasible but in Warrington, considering the number Of works, they /east put up with the smoke. The MAYOR said that Councillor Bennett was quite in order in bringing the matter forward as the report of Mr Church was bound with that of the Medical Officer. The minutes were then confirmed. A Catastrophe Averted.

Aldetman HEATOS proposed the minutes of the Paving and Sewerage Committee, and referred to a report pre- pared by the Borough Surveyor in regard to the bleak- down of the compressors in Mersey-street- The report states that the compressors were fixed in 1882 for the purposes of the Latchford drainage. At that time the contents of about 430,000 pails were forwarded .per annum' whereas there are now 684,000 pails to be dealt with. The Surveyor recommended that the Sanitary Works Committee be asked to start their new compres— Sor(4. V. hich had been fixed at the Etectricity Station at the earliest possible moment. Councillor TURNION seconded, and said he should like to emploasiz-? what bad been said with regard to the compressors. They had twice hrken down in the last few weeks, and the Corporation was exceedingly fortu- tunate in not having bad a serious accident, consider- lag lag the time the compressors had n working. Councillor JOHN EVANS said oil alf of the Sanitary k Works Committee that they Wry ad the compressors fixed now to several months, and they were only wait- ing for special pipes to connect them with the boilers. Mr Dells had had a definite promise that the pipes would be here this week. Immediately the pipes were con- nected the compressors would be put on. They were also going Ca couple them on to those compressors at Mersey-street. (Hear, hear). Alderman 11E4TON : We Jo not blame the Sanitary Committee at all. .
The minutes were passed. School Attendance.

The committee, he ssid also recommended the substitution of the following bye-law in place of the one relating to children between the ages al3 years and 14 years. After having completed 250 attendances during a period from let November to 31st May, or sub- st-quent thereto, be exempt from further attendances until I<t November next ensuing. C uucllor Piano= seconded and the minutes were confirmed. -

div.head: Water Works Extensions.
div.p: The Water Works Extensions.
Alderman Francamb Reports Progress.

In proposing the adoption of the minutes of the Water Committee, Alderman Franconab made a statement in regard to the progress of the extension, about which questions were ask.cl at the laA Council meeting. He stated that the waterworks were purchased 11 years ago, when the water pumped per day amounted to 900,000 gallons. They now pumped 600,000 gallons per day, the consumption hav- ing alrnos.. doubled. A year or two ago it was decided Ito extend the woiks very largely and the committee were at the present moment doing their utmost to carry ! out the work satisfactorily. Those extensions consisted of several independent portions. They had an enormous rese.vAr at Win wick which was twice the size of the one in use, and which would hold 4i million gallons of water. They had no extra well, out down Delph- ilane, towards Middleton, they had the first ' and the principal one of four new shafts. This shalt was down 160 feet and promised an ample supply of water. They were now pumping 500,000 ma, lons a day from it, but at present the water had to be allowed to run waste. From this shaft they loaa had to lay a rising main to Winwick, about 1i miles where the new reservoir was situated. That reservoir was rapidly nearing completion: Another shaft was sunk 1,200 yards from the No 1 Abaft . and this was down 102 feet and was yielding 220,000 gallons per day,also running io waste. Number 3 hatt was another 1,200 yards away, but was only sunk 501 t, while number 4 shaft was sunk 301 t. Neither of these two as yet yielded water, but there was every reason to Oclieve that as they got down there would be an abund- ance of water. Those shafts were all connected with the one at D- Iph-lane, from whence the water was to be taken to vVinwick, and then forced up to the highest point at Hill Warren where the new receiving reseivoir was made to hold one million gallons. To this point they had to lay a main 6i miles long, the town portion of which had to be lain during the night time. When they had got the water up at Hill Warren they would le able to supply the whole of the surrounding district. At the present time they had got work going on which involved an outlay of £So.OOO. Everything was proceeding satisfactorily in their efforts to increase the domestic supply. Eventually they hoped to be able to provide Ltbandantly tor the traders of the town, and also so as to encourage other manufacturers to settle down in Warrington. Councillor JOHN EVANS seconded. Councillor ELLISON asked when the Water Committee was going to be able to give a better supply of water for the streets of Latchford. There had been many com- plaints for a long time,
Councillor linrcrox thought the information given was very satisfactory, but he would like to know when the operations would be completed, and when they might txpect a beLter supply of water. _ .

„- Alderman FRANCO= replied to the questions, and siid that the Water Committee was unable to give tbe Pav- ing and Sewerage Commttee the water they required for the streets, because they did not want to touch ‘Vinwick water for this purpose, He thought they had better pay more for carting than the public be short of water. Replying to Councillor Burton. the Alderman said the reservoir would be ready in a very short time.

div.head: Tramways Corn mittee—The Light Railway.
div.p: Tramways Corn mittee—The Light Railway.

The Mania proposed the minutes of the Tramways Committee which stated that the p:oinoters of the War- rington and Northwich Light Railway had signed the agreement as amended, by which the Corporation have secured the option of purchasing Railway No lat cost price plus 5 per cent for supervision, and the cost of incidental works authorised by the order. The agree- ment also provides:that the promoters shall:take electric power from the Corporation with a minimum con- sumption of 200,000 units per annum. The MAYOR remarked that the object of the arrange- ment was to enable the town at the prop( r ,iirre to acquire that portion of the Light Railway which was connected with th iir tramways on the south side at Stockton Heath Swing bridge and thus enable them tp make a complete circuit to Warrington by way of Li chford. Ile also submitted to the consideration of the Cauncil an application to the Board of Trade for sanction to borrow £66,050 for tho construction of tramways from Liverpool-road to Knutsford-road and along Wilderspool Causeway. This figure was based upon the estimate submitted by ,Messrs Preece and Car- dew, and so far as the first part of the work was con- cerned the tenders had come v.-Ty near the estimate. This could not, he added, los colisidered short notice to those gentlemen who were so anxious to air their abilities and disaoilities about the affairs of the town. Councillor Mimi:is alluded to the estimate for the tramways mentioned, and drew attention to the large amount (£39,000) to be spent on the permanent way. He supposed this provided for the laying down of the rails, taking up and carting away the old setts and macadam, laying fresh sett, cost of labour, etc. He could not understand how it was, but he knew that engineers always insisted upsn taking up an old sett which in some instances was better than the new one they were going to lay down. He specified Wininarleigh- street, where he said the sett paving was the best in Warrington, and the setts better than any they could put down now. According to some engineers they would , not do because they were four inch cubes, and setts ot from 6 inches to 10 inches were r,.quired. He under- stood that in many t.iwas the iliinch cube was used,but only in towns where the Corporation had had their own engineer to superintend. Elo did not think they fared any better by going far afield for ,ladvice in thia matter. If they would reckon up he , thought they would find that some £6,000 was going to be wssted if the engineer preferred to take up the exist- ing four inch cubes and replace them by setts of six or ten inches. This would be a gross waste of public money. He disapproved of engkeers' commission being paid on the lump sum spent because it miht, he did not say it did, tempt them to swell their estimates. Five per cent on £6,000 would go into the pockets of the ei gineers if they advised the substitution of new sets for the old ones. He thought the tramways could be laid and the setts which had been taken up used again, and protested against unnecessary expenditure. Councillor BENNETT asked why Manchester-read had not had a prior claim for the tramways. It had neither bridges nor level crossing, and he hoped the claims of the district would not be lost sight of. Councillor JAMES EVANS supported the observations at Councillor Tinnion. Hs did not think they stionld altogether be guided by consulting engineers in the matters of this sort when they had an engineer of their wen. He understood that when constructed and before they were used, the tramways would be inspected by a Government Inspector, and they ought to know whether there would be any risk of them being rejected should they depart from the advice of the engineers. He would move a resolution.—
The MAYOR : I must remind you that the tender was accepted at our last meeting for permanent way and overhead equipment. _

Councillor EVANS That only confirms my observa- tions that we are frequently passing important resolu- tions which we should not have passed on second con- sideration. The question was not raised previously as to the using of old material.
The MAYOEI : IL is only an expression Jf opinion and capable of explanation.

Alderman SUTTON: This is simply an application for the borrowing of the money. If it should be found after- . wards that there is a good deal in what Councillor Tinnion has said we should do our best to pr t vent the spendinglof the money. An inspector will be down before long to go into the application, Alderman Straw GREEN advised a pause for sufficient consideration to be given to CJuncillor Tinnion's re- marks. Lie presumed the remarks had been made only as the visult of information from those" in the know." The Murcia considered it a little bit late in the day to suggest with reference to slessrs Preece and Cardew, who were appointed the engineers of the work niany. months ago, that. the Corporation might have done better if they had had somebody nearer home. The appointment of these gentlemen was the appointment of the Council, and it was a little bit superfluous to criticise an appointment made long a.:2. Dealing with the question As to whether it was pi siible to use up existing setts, the Nlayor promised that the attention of the engineers would be drawn to the matter, and if it was possible to use the existing setts, they would be used and a corresponding reduction made from the tender accepted. Proceeding to refer to the financial aspect of the tramways, his worship said they had to discuss it in the light of the experience of other towns and the report of Messrs Preeee and Cardew gave figures showing what was the necessary revenue for succetsful financial results. All the Tramways Committee could do was to endeav- our to secure the necessary revenue. If this system of locomotion did not appeal to the people of Warrington for support, they would have to pay for it through the rates. The contract for oars had not yet been -ccepted I and the commit e hail cot yet ilecclPd upon the pattern. The commit ee h pod to come to satisfactory terms with the Gas Committe for a car shed to b. placed on their premises in Mersey-street. The Gas Committee had got a lot of land there wi ich he understood was worth very little and they wruld be diqyieel to treat the Tramways Con mitten in a liberal spirit. As to Wilderepool Cam a way no tender had been accepted, but theestimate was based on that already accepted for the Liverpool-road line. Mr Councillor Bennett had very properly raised the question of the desirability of making the

Manchester-road tramway and be thought other members of the Council might just as properly I have refered to the advisaidlity of a Winwick•road tramway. He did not think they would like to witness the prospect of the inconveLience that would be caused in having the roads of the whole town pulled op at one time. Another reason was that the Council would like to have someresults from some p3rtion of the tramways scheme before the whole of the capital was expended. The committee preferred to do it in sections and to be guided by the results obtained. (Hear. hear). the minutes were then passed. The Deputy Town Clerk.

The General Purposes Committee recommended that the aalary of Mr Stanley Wilson, the Deputy Town Clerk, be increased to £250 per annum, wirh an addi- tional increase of £25 per anaum, up to a maximum of £3Ol.

The MAYOII moved the confirmation of the minutes, and in referring to the inerease of salary, he expr, aged the opinion that Mr Wilson had n( t been over abundantly/ paid for the valuable services he had rendered for many years past. There was another reascn why his position should receive consideration and that was the fact that he had become a qualified solici- tor and therefore capable of rendering much more im- portant cervices and of more value financially, and in many other respects becoming a much more able and important servant than he had previously been. Mr Wil4on had always shown assiduity and etention to his duties and great courteiy to everyone with whom be came in contact. The Mayor proceeded to congratu• late Mr Sutcliffe, the Deputy BorouglA Surveyor on his appointment as assistant surveyor to the Lambeth Council. The minutes were then approved.
